teile.einleitung: Sultanism is a term from political science. It describes a form of rule in which a ruler treats the state like his private property and governs entirely as he pleases.
wichtigste: The term was coined by the sociologist Max Weber.
Mixing up state property and private property is typical.
Loyalty is based on fear and reward, not on an ideology.
Power is often passed on within the family.
Examples are Trujillo, the Duvaliers and the Somozas.
Ceaușescu's regime also showed sultanistic features.

abschnitte.text: The German sociologist **Max Weber** described different forms of rule in his work “Economy and Society”. He called rule that is based entirely on the **free will** of the ruler **sultanistic**. He saw it as an extreme form of **patrimonial rule**, in which the ruler runs the state like a household. Later researchers such as **Juan Linz** and **Alfred Stepan** applied the term to modern dictatorships.

In sultanism there is hardly any boundary between **state property** and **private property**. The ruler and his family enrich themselves from the country. Supporters stay loyal to him out of **fear** or because of **rewards**, not because of a world view. Family members often hold important posts. There is often a strong **personality cult**.

**Rafael Trujillo** ruled the Dominican Republic and had the capital Santo Domingo called **Ciudad Trujillo** from 1936 to 1961. He was murdered in 1961. In **Haiti**, **François “Papa Doc” Duvalier** relied on the feared militia, the **Tontons Macoutes**. His son Jean-Claude took power in 1971 and was overthrown in 1986. In **Nicaragua**, the **Somoza family** ruled the country like a family possession until 1979.

In **Turkmenistan**, **Saparmurat Niyazov** had himself called “Turkmenbashi” and named months after himself and his mother. He ruled until his death in 2006. Linz and Stepan described the regime of **Nicolae Ceaușescu** in Romania as a mixture of totalitarianism and sultanism. Ceaușescu and his wife Elena were executed on 25 December 1989.

gewusst: The name comes from the title “sultan” but has nothing to do with any particular religion or region.
Trujillo even named his country's capital after himself.

teile.einleitung: In Spain, the “Transición” is the name for the transition from Franco's dictatorship to democracy. It began after Franco's death in 1975 and was largely peaceful.
wichtigste: “Transición” is Spanish for “transition”.
After Franco's death in 1975, Juan Carlos I became king.
As prime minister, Adolfo Suárez led the reforms.
In 1977 there were the first free elections for more than 40 years.
In 1978 Spain got a democratic constitution.
A coup attempt in 1981 failed.

abschnitte.text: General **Francisco Franco** ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975. Two days later **Juan Carlos I** became king. Many expected him to continue Franco's policies. But he helped to make Spain a **democracy**. In 1976 he appointed **Adolfo Suárez** prime minister. Suárez pushed through important reforms.

On **15 June 1977**, the people of Spain were allowed to vote freely for the first time in more than 40 years. Many parties were allowed again. In October 1977 the government and the parties concluded the **Moncloa Pacts**, named after the seat of government in Madrid. In them they agreed on joint economic reforms. On **6 December 1978** the people approved the new **constitution**. Today this day is a public holiday.

On **23 February 1981**, armed men of the **Guardia Civil** stormed the parliament in Madrid. They wanted to take power. In a **television address**, the king clearly backed democracy. After that the plotters gave up. The attempt had failed by the next day.

Today Spain is a **parliamentary monarchy**. The king is head of state, and the people elect parliament. In 1986 Spain, together with Portugal, joined the **European Community**, today's EU. This was only possible because both countries had become democracies.

gewusst: In many countries the Transición is seen as an example of a peaceful way out of a dictatorship.
Opponents of the government also took part in the Moncloa Pacts.

teile.einleitung: The Khmer Rouge were a communist movement in Cambodia. Under their leader Pol Pot they ruled from 1975 to 1979 and caused the deaths of about a quarter of the population.
wichtigste: On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge captured the capital, Phnom Penh.
Their state was called Democratic Kampuchea.
The cities were forcibly emptied, and the people were driven into the countryside.
An estimated 1.5 to 2 million people died.
Thousands were killed in the S-21 prison, Tuol Sleng.
In January 1979 Vietnam ended their rule with an invasion.

abschnitte.text: After years of civil war, the **Khmer Rouge** marched into **Phnom Penh** on **17 April 1975**. Their leader was **Pol Pot**. They called their state **Democratic Kampuchea**. The leadership remained secret for a long time, and people had to obey the **Angkar**, “the Organisation”, without question.

The Khmer Rouge wanted to create a **classless farming society** and start everything anew, from **“Year Zero”**. Immediately after taking power, they had the cities **forcibly emptied**. Millions of people had to go to the countryside and do hard work there. Money, schools, markets and religion were abolished. Educated people were seen as enemies.

Through executions, **forced labour**, hunger and disease, an estimated **1.5 to 2 million people** died. That was about a quarter of the population. In the torture prison **S-21**, in a former school called **Tuol Sleng**, thousands of people were held prisoner, and almost all of them were killed. Today there is a museum there. The nearby execution site is called Choeung Ek.

After border conflicts, **Vietnam** attacked Cambodia. On **7 January 1979**, Vietnamese troops took Phnom Penh. The Khmer Rouge withdrew into the jungle on the Thai border and carried on fighting for many years. Pol Pot died in 1998 without ever having been convicted.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: In 2010 a special court supported by the UN, the **Khmer Rouge Tribunal**, convicted its first defendant, **Duch**, the head of S-21. His sentence was later increased to life imprisonment. Other leading Khmer Rouge figures were also convicted. The 1984 film **“The Killing Fields”** made the crimes known all over the world.

gewusst: The title “The Killing Fields” became the term for Cambodia's mass graves.
Only very few of the prisoners in S-21 survived.

teile.einleitung: Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya is an opposition politician from Belarus. In 2020 she stood against Alexander Lukashenko in the presidential election and became the face of the democracy movement.
wichtigste: Tsikhanouskaya comes from Belarus.
She stood for election in 2020 because her husband had been arrested.
Her opponent was Alexander Lukashenko, who has ruled since 1994.
After the election she had to flee to Lithuania.
The opposition received the Sakharov Prize in 2020.
Her husband Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released in June 2025.

abschnitte.text: Before 2020, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was hardly known politically. Her husband, the blogger **Siarhei Tsikhanouski**, wanted to stand in the presidential election and was arrested. So she stood in his place. Other male candidates were also eliminated. As a result, three women led the campaign together: **Tsikhanouskaya**, **Maria Kalesnikava** and **Veronika Tsepkalo**.

**Alexander Lukashenko** has ruled Belarus in an authoritarian way since **1994**. In 2020, despite accusations of fraud, he had himself declared the winner of the election. After that there were the largest protests in the country's history. Many demonstrators carried the **white-red-white flag**. It was the flag of independent Belarus in the 1990s and became the symbol of the opposition.

Under pressure from the authorities, Tsikhanouskaya had to leave Belarus after the election. She went to **Lithuania** and lived in the capital **Vilnius**. From there she continues to campaign for a democratic Belarus. She meets governments in many countries and asks for support.

In 2020 the **European Parliament** awarded the **Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought** to the democratic opposition in Belarus. Her husband Siarhei Tsikhanouski spent around five years in prison. In **June 2025** he was released and was able to leave for Lithuania.

gewusst: Tsikhanouskaya became a politician without having planned to, because her husband was not allowed to stand.
A well-known picture from 2020 shows the three women of the opposition with a heart, a fist and a victory sign.

teile.einleitung: Saparmurat Niyazov ruled Turkmenistan in Central Asia from 1985 until his death in 2006. He built up one of the strangest personality cults in the world and had himself called “Turkmenbashi”, leader of the Turkmens.
wichtigste: From 1985 Niyazov led the Communist Party of the Turkmen Soviet Republic.
After independence in 1991 he became president.
In 1995 the UN recognised Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality.
In 1999 he became president for life.
In Ashgabat a golden statue of him turned with the sun.
After his death in 2006, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow followed him.

abschnitte.text: In 1985 **Saparmurat Niyazov** became **First Secretary** of the Communist Party of the Turkmen Soviet Republic. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Turkmenistan became independent. Niyazov stayed in power without a break, now as **President**. In **1999** parliament made him **president for life**. After that, no presidential elections were held until his death.

On **12 December 1995**, the **UN General Assembly** recognised Turkmenistan's **permanent neutrality**. The country did not want to join any alliance, similar to Switzerland. In the capital **Ashgabat**, the huge **Neutrality Arch** was a reminder of this. On top stood a gilded statue of Niyazov that turned so that it always faced the sun.

Niyazov had himself called **Turkmenbashi**. Pictures of him hung everywhere. He wrote a book called the **Ruhnama**, which was compulsory reading in schools. He even had the names of months changed: January was named after him, and April after his mother. Criticism was not allowed, and opponents were persecuted.

Niyazov considered **opera** and **ballet** “un-Turkmen” and had the company dissolved in 2001. In **2005** he ordered the **hospitals outside the capital** to be closed. Sick people were to come to Ashgabat. As a result, health care for the rural population became much worse.

Niyazov died in **December 2006**. His successor was the former health minister **Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow**. He reversed some of the orders, for example the new names of the months. The golden statue was moved to the edge of the city. But Berdimuhamedow also built up a personality cult.

gewusst: Turkmenistan has huge reserves of natural gas.
During Niyazov's lifetime, towns, streets and schools were named after him.

teile.einleitung: Schoolbooks help children to learn new things. In Switzerland they are often called teaching materials. What is in schoolbooks matters, because they shape how children see the world.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, schoolbooks are often called teaching materials.
They are free at state schools.
The cantons decide which teaching materials are used.
In a democracy, schoolbooks should give objective information.
In dictatorships, schoolbooks often praise the ruler.
You can borrow many more books from the library.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, schoolbooks are often called **teaching materials**. These also include **workbooks**, in which children do exercises, and more and more digital resources. At **state schools**, teaching materials are **free**. This is because the **Federal Constitution** promises free primary education.

In Switzerland, state schools are the responsibility of the **cantons**. They decide which teaching materials are used in schools. Many cantons work together on this. In the German-speaking cantons, the teaching materials follow **Lehrplan 21**, the curriculum. It sets out what children should learn at what age.

In a **democracy**, schoolbooks should give **objective** and **true** information. On controversial questions they show different opinions. Children should learn to think for themselves and form their own view. That is why teaching materials are carefully checked and revised again and again.

In **dictatorships**, schoolbooks are often written so that the ruler looks good. Mistakes and crimes of the government are hushed up, and opponents are made to look bad. This is a form of **propaganda**. In this way children are meant to learn early on to obey the government. In North Korea, for example, schoolbooks praise the ruling family.

If you read different books, you get to know **different points of view**. In the **library** you can borrow books free of charge or very cheaply. This gives everyone access to knowledge, no matter how much money they have. It is a good addition to the schoolbook.

gewusst: One of the first schoolbooks with pictures was written by John Amos Comenius in the 17th century.
Some Swiss cantons have their own publishers for teaching materials.

teile.einleitung: The Somoza family ruled Nicaragua from the 1930s until 1979. Three members of the family were president, and the family owned a large part of the country's economy.
wichtigste: The Somoza family ruled Nicaragua in Central America.
Three Somozas were president: a father and two sons.
The founder Anastasio Somoza García was shot dead in an assassination in 1956.
After the 1972 earthquake, the family enriched itself from aid money.
In 1979 the Sandinistas overthrew the dictatorship.
The last dictator was killed in exile in Paraguay in 1980.

abschnitte.text: **Anastasio Somoza García** came to power in the 1930s. After his death his sons **Luis** and **Anastasio Somoza Debayle** ruled one after the other. That is why people speak of a **family dynasty**. The Somozas owned companies, land and factories. So they controlled not only politics but also a large part of the economy.

In 1972 a severe **earthquake** destroyed the capital **Managua** and killed thousands of people. Help came from many countries. But a large part of the international aid money disappeared into the pockets of the family and their trusted associates. This made many people angry, including some who had previously supported the Somozas.

**Pedro Joaquín Chamorro** was the publisher of the newspaper “La Prensa” and a sharp critic of Somoza. In January 1978 he was murdered. After that there were large protests and **general strikes**. The **Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN)** led the armed uprising. It is named after **Augusto César Sandino**, who had fought against the US occupation and was murdered in 1934 on Somoza García's orders.

On **19 July 1979**, the Sandinista fighters entered Managua. Anastasio Somoza Debayle had fled shortly before. He finally found refuge with the dictator **Alfredo Stroessner** in **Asunción**, the capital of Paraguay. There he was killed in an attack in September 1980.

gewusst: The Sandinistas bear the name of a rebel whom the founder of the dynasty had murdered.
In Nicaragua, 19 July is marked as the Day of the Revolution.

teile.einleitung: Rosa Parks was a Black woman from the USA. Because she would not give up her seat on a bus to a white man in 1955, she was arrested. Her courage helped to end unjust racial segregation.
wichtigste: On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks stayed in her seat on a bus in Montgomery.
She was arrested and had to pay a fine.
After that, many Black people boycotted the buses for more than a year.
Martin Luther King became famous as the leader of the boycott.
Rosa Parks is regarded as the “mother of the civil rights movement”.

abschnitte.text: In many southern states of the USA, there used to be laws on **racial segregation**. Black and white people had to use separate schools, toilets and seats on the bus. In **Montgomery** in the state of **Alabama**, Black people had to give up their seats if a white person could not find a seat. Many people found this deeply unjust.

abschnitte.titel: Rosa Parks stays in her seat
abschnitte.text: **Rosa Parks** worked as a seamstress and had long campaigned for the rights of Black people. On **1 December 1955**, she was told to stand up on the bus for a white passenger. She refused and calmly stayed in her seat. She was then **arrested** by the police and had to pay a **fine**.

After her arrest, many Black people in Montgomery decided not to travel by bus any more. They walked or shared cars. This **bus boycott** lasted more than **380 days**, so more than a year. The bus company lost a lot of money. It only ended when the Supreme Court of the USA had banned segregation on the buses.

The boycott was led by the young minister **Martin Luther King**. He relied on **non-violent resistance**. Through the boycott he became known throughout the USA. Later he became one of the most important leaders of the **civil rights movement**, which fought for equal rights for all people.

abschnitte.titel: Mother of the civil rights movement
abschnitte.text: Her brave behaviour gave many people the strength to stand up for their rights. That is why Rosa Parks is called the **mother of the civil rights movement**. She later received high honours from the USA. When she died in 2005, she lay in honour in the Capitol in Washington, a special distinction.

gewusst: Rosa Parks was the first woman to lie in honour in the Capitol in Washington.
The bus on which Rosa Parks stayed in her seat is now in a museum near Detroit.

teile.einleitung: In dictatorships, some books are banned because those in power fear the ideas in them. Anyone who writes, prints or reads such books can be punished. Famous examples are the book burnings of 1933 in Germany and the texts that were spread in secret in the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: Dictatorships ban books because they contain unwelcome ideas.
On 10 May 1933 the National Socialists publicly burned books in Berlin and many other cities.
Erich Kästner watched in Berlin as his own books were burned.
Blacklists named authors whose books were to disappear from libraries.
In the Soviet Union, banned texts were secretly copied out and passed on as **samizdat**.
George Orwell's novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four” was banned in the Soviet Union until the end of the 1980s.
Anyone who owned banned books could be arrested.

abschnitte.text: Shortly after taking power, the National Socialists had books burned in many cities on **10 May 1933**. Students threw into the fire the works of authors whom the regime rejected, for example Jewish, left-wing or pacifist writers. In Berlin this happened in what is now **Bebelplatz**. The children's author **Erich Kästner** stood in the crowd and watched his own books burn. Many of the writers affected then fled abroad.

The National Socialists drew up **blacklists** of unwanted authors and books. These books were removed from libraries and bookshops. Publishers were no longer allowed to print them. In this way people were only supposed to read what fitted the views of those in power. This control over books, newspapers and films is called **censorship**.

Many books were also banned in the Soviet Union, for example George Orwell's novel **“Nineteen Eighty-Four”**. It describes a state that watches everyone. Brave people typed out banned texts on typewriters and secretly passed the copies on. This was called **samizdat**, which means “self-publishing”. Anyone who was caught could expect to be punished.

In dictatorships it was dangerous to own banned books. Anyone caught with them could be **arrested**. That is why many people hid such books well or only read them in secret. Some authors published their works abroad so that they could appear at all. In Switzerland, for example, books by authors who were banned in Germany were published in the 1930s.

In **Bebelplatz** in Berlin a special memorial remembers the book burning. Under a glass plate in the ground you can see **empty bookshelves**. They would have room for around 20,000 books, about as many as were burned there. The empty shelves show what was lost. Today, in democracies like Switzerland, the freedom to write and read books is seen as an important right.

gewusst: Erich Kästner was probably the only author who himself watched his books being burned in Berlin.
You can only see the memorial in Bebelplatz if you look down through the glass plate.
Samizdat was often typed with carbon paper, so several copies were made at once.

teile.einleitung: The time of National Socialism in Germany lasted from 1933 to 1945. During this time Adolf Hitler ruled as a dictator, and his party, the NSDAP, controlled the whole country. It was one of the darkest periods in history, with the Second World War and the genocide of six million Jews.
wichtigste: Adolf Hitler ruled Germany as a dictator from 1933 to 1945.
On 30 January 1933 Hitler became Reich Chancellor, and he then abolished democracy within a short time.
The National Socialists persecuted Jews, Sinti and Roma, political opponents and many other groups.
In the Holocaust, about six million Jews were murdered.
The Second World War in Europe began with the attack on Poland on 1 September 1939.
On 8 May 1945 Germany surrendered unconditionally.
Switzerland stayed neutral but was surrounded by Germany and its allies.

abschnitte.text: The Nazi era began on 30 January 1933, when Adolf Hitler was appointed **Reich Chancellor**. It ended on 8 May 1945 with Germany's surrender. During the war, Germany occupied large parts of Europe, from France to deep inside the Soviet Union. Hitler called his state the “Third Reich”.

After the First World War, many Germans suffered from poverty, unemployment and a feeling of humiliation. The **Great Depression** from 1929 made the hardship even worse. Hitler and his party, the NSDAP, promised simple solutions and made Jews and others scapegoats. In elections in 1932 the NSDAP became the strongest party, but it never had a majority on its own.

As early as 1933, the **Enabling Act** gave Hitler the power to pass laws without parliament. Other parties were banned, trade unions dissolved and the press controlled; this was called **Gleichschaltung** (bringing into line). The secret police, the Gestapo, persecuted opponents, who were locked up in concentration camps. Children and young people had to join the Hitler Youth or the League of German Girls.

Step by step, the National Socialists took away the rights of the Jews, for example with the Nuremberg Laws of 1935. During the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, synagogues burned everywhere. During the war, the Nazis systematically murdered millions of people in extermination camps such as **Auschwitz**. This genocide is called the **Holocaust** or Shoah; Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities and many others also became victims.

Switzerland stayed **neutral** in the Second World War and was not attacked. General Henri Guisan had the army prepare to defend itself in the Alps, in the so-called Réduit. Switzerland took in refugees, but it also turned away many Jewish refugees at the border. The St Gallen police commander Paul Grüninger saved hundreds of Jews by breaking the rules, and he was dismissed for it.

More than 60 million people died worldwide in the Second World War. After the war, leading Nazis were convicted at the **Nuremberg trials**, and Germany was divided. Today it is forbidden in Germany and Switzerland to deny the Holocaust. Memorials and school lessons help people remember, so that something like this never happens again.

begriffe.erklaerung: National Socialist German Workers' Party, Hitler's party.
The genocide of the European Jews by the National Socialists.
Bringing all areas of society into line with Nazi ideology.
Camps in which the Nazis locked up, tormented and murdered people.
Brave people who fought back against the dictatorship.

gewusst: The student Sophie Scholl of the White Rose resistance group was executed in 1943 at only 21 years of age.
On 20 July 1944, Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg tried to kill Hitler with a bomb.
Paul Grüninger was only rehabilitated by a court in 1995, long after his death.

teile.einleitung: A truth commission investigates which crimes were committed during a dictatorship or a civil war. It collects witness statements and evidence and writes a report. Many countries in Latin America and Africa have set up such commissions.
wichtigste: A truth commission investigates the crimes of a dictatorship but is not a court.
The Argentine report “Nunca más” of 1984 means “Never again”.
The Argentine commission CONADEP was led by the writer Ernesto Sabato.
In Chile there was the Rettig Commission of 1990 and later the Valech Commission.
In 2003 the commission in Peru established around 69,000 deaths.
Brazil presented a final report in 2014.
The South African commission under Desmond Tutu became known worldwide.

abschnitte.text: A **truth commission** collects **witness statements** and evidence about human rights violations. It hears victims and relatives and searches through files. At the end it writes a public **report**. It is **not a court** and does not convict anyone. But its reports often help in later trials.

After the end of the military dictatorship, President **Raúl Alfonsín** set up the **CONADEP** commission in 1983. It was led by the respected writer **Ernesto Sabato**. In 1984 its report **“Nunca más”** was published, which means “Never again”. It documented thousands of cases of disappeared people. The report became a bestseller.

In Chile the National Commission for Truth and Reconciliation was set up in 1990. It is called the **Rettig Commission** after its chairman, the lawyer **Raúl Rettig**. It investigated deaths and disappearances under the Pinochet dictatorship. In 2003 and 2004 the **Valech Commission** heard tens of thousands of former political prisoners. Its report confirmed that **torture** had been used systematically.

In 1993 a commission set up by the UN presented the report “From Madness to Hope” for **El Salvador**. In **Guatemala** the report “Memory of Silence” was published in 1999. It concluded that the state had committed **genocide** against Maya communities. In 2003 the commission in **Peru** established around 69,000 deaths in the conflict with rebels such as the “Shining Path”. **Brazil** presented a report in 2014 that named 434 people who had been killed or had disappeared.

The commission in **South Africa** became especially well known. Under Archbishop **Desmond Tutu**, it investigated the crimes of apartheid from 1996. It placed a strong emphasis on reconciliation. Many countries were influenced by it and by the Latin American commissions. Today truth commissions are regarded as an important tool when a country makes a new start after a dictatorship.

gewusst: The report “Nunca más” became one of the best-selling books in Argentina.
According to the commission, the victims in Peru were mostly poor indigenous farmers, and many spoke Quechua.

teile.einleitung: In 2020 a new security law came into force in Hong Kong. It was passed in Beijing and has greatly restricted freedoms in the city.
wichtigste: Hong Kong was a British colony for a long time and has been part of China again since 1997.
The principle “One country, two systems” was meant to secure Hong Kong's own freedoms until 2047.
The security law was passed in Beijing in 2020, without Hong Kong's parliament.
The maximum penalty is life imprisonment.
It was preceded by the mass protests of 2019.
The critical newspaper Apple Daily had to close in 2021.

abschnitte.text: Hong Kong was a **British colony** for more than 150 years. In 1997 Great Britain returned the city to the **People's Republic of China**. China promised the principle of **“One country, two systems”**. Hong Kong was to keep its own legal and economic system until 2047. This included freedom of expression, freedom of the press and independent courts.

In 2014 many people demanded freer elections. They protected themselves against police pepper spray with umbrellas, which is why the protests are called the **Umbrella Movement**. In 2019 there were even larger **mass protests**, first against an extradition law and then for more democracy. According to the organisers, up to two million people took to the streets.

In June 2020 the **Standing Committee of the National People's Congress** in Beijing passed the security law. Hong Kong's own parliament was bypassed. The law punishes **subversion**, **secession**, **terrorism** and **collusion with foreign countries**. In serious cases, **life imprisonment** is possible. The terms are broadly defined, which is why peaceful critics can also be affected.

After the law, many activists and politicians of the democracy movement were arrested or left the country. Jimmy Lai's newspaper **Apple Daily** was critical of Beijing. After raids and the freezing of its accounts, it had to close in June 2021. The activist **Joshua Wong**, who was already well known as a school pupil, was also convicted under the security law in 2024.

The Chinese government says that the law brought back **peace and order** after the unrest. Critics, many Western governments and human rights organisations see it as the end of “One country, two systems”. They complain that freedom of expression and freedom of the press have been greatly restricted. Switzerland has also expressed concern about the developments.

gewusst: In 2014 the umbrella became the symbol of the Hong Kong protests.
The 2019 protests were among the largest in Hong Kong's history.

teile.einleitung: A theocracy is a form of state in which rule is exercised in the name of God or a religion. Religious leaders or laws stand above worldly institutions.
wichtigste: The word “theocracy” means “rule by God”.
The term was coined by the ancient historian Flavius Josephus.
If priests actually rule, it is called a hierocracy.
Since 1979 Iran has been based on the “guardianship of the jurist”.
In old Tibet, the Dalai Lama was both spiritual and worldly leader.
Calvin's Geneva is seen as an example of a city strongly shaped by the church.

abschnitte.text: The word **theocracy** comes from Greek: “theos” means God, and “kratia” rule. The Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** used it in his work “Against Apion”. With it he described the constitution of Israel as rule by God. A related term is **hierocracy**, from the Greek “hieros” for holy. It stresses that priests actually rule.

After the revolution of 1979, the principle of **“Velayat-e faqih”** was written into Iran's constitution. It means “guardianship of the jurist” and goes back to **Khomeini**. A supreme religious jurist stands above the elected bodies. The **Guardian Council**, with twelve members, checks laws and helps decide who may stand in elections. The **Assembly of Experts** chooses the Supreme Leader.

From 1541 the reformer **John Calvin** shaped the city of **Geneva**. With the **“Ordonnances ecclésiastiques”** (church ordinances), he set up a **Consistory** that watched over the lives of the citizens. Formally, however, the city council remained the worldly authority. In 1553 the council sentenced the Spanish doctor and theologian **Michael Servetus** to death because he denied the Trinity. Calvin agreed with the verdict.

In **Tibet**, the **Ganden Phodrang** government united religious and political leadership. At its head was the **Dalai Lama**. In 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama fled to **India**. He has lived in exile ever since. Today Tibet is part of the People's Republic of China.

In many democracies, including Switzerland, **state and religion** are separate or at least clearly distinguished. **Freedom of religion** is protected in the Federal Constitution. In a theocracy, on the other hand, religion decides the laws. People who believe differently or do not believe often have fewer rights.

gewusst: The word theocracy is almost 2000 years old.
In 1989 the Iranian Assembly of Experts chose Khomeini's successor.

teile.einleitung: Wolf Biermann is a German singer-songwriter and poet. As a young man he moved to the GDR of his own free will, but there he criticised the government in his songs. In 1976 the GDR stripped him of his citizenship, which caused great protests.
wichtigste: Wolf Biermann was born in Hamburg in 1936 and moved to the GDR in 1953.
From 1965 he was no longer allowed to perform in public in the GDR.
In 1968 his album “Chausseestrasse 131” was released in the West.
In November 1976 he gave a concert in Cologne.
On 16 November 1976 the GDR stripped him of his citizenship.
Many artists protested against this in an open letter.
Manfred Krug left the GDR afterwards, and Robert Havemann was put under house arrest.

abschnitte.text: Wolf Biermann was born in **Hamburg in 1936**. He grew up in a communist family. His father was murdered in **Auschwitz** in 1943. As a teenager, Biermann moved to the GDR of his own free will in **1953**. He wanted to help build a socialist state there.

Biermann wrote songs and poems in which he criticised the GDR's leadership. After a meeting of the SED Central Committee in December **1965**, he was **banned from performing and publishing**. After that his songs only appeared in the West. Because he was not allowed to perform, he recorded them in his flat in East Berlin. He named the 1968 album after the address: **“Chausseestrasse 131”**.

In November 1976 Biermann was surprisingly allowed to travel to the West. On **13 November 1976**, at the invitation of the IG Metall trade union, he performed in the **Cologne sports hall**. The concert was broadcast on television and was also seen in the GDR. Three days later, on **16 November 1976**, the GDR took away his citizenship. He was not allowed to return. This is called **expatriation**.

On **17 November 1976**, well-known artists such as **Christa Wolf**, **Stefan Heym** and Heiner Müller asked in an **open letter** for the measure to be reconsidered. More than a hundred others joined them. Many were punished for this. The actor and singer **Manfred Krug** hardly got any more roles and moved to West Berlin in 1977. Biermann's friend, the chemist **Robert Havemann**, was under **house arrest** from 1976 to 1979.

The expatriation is regarded as an important turning point in the history of the GDR. Afterwards many artists left the country. Many people's trust in the government fell. From then on Biermann lived in the West and carried on performing. In **1991** he received the **Georg Büchner Prize**, one of Germany's most important literary prizes.

gewusst: Biermann was stripped of his citizenship precisely while he was on a permitted concert tour in the West.
After his expatriation, Biermann moved back to Hamburg, the city where he was born.

teile.einleitung: A show trial is a public court case whose verdict has already been decided beforehand. It does not serve justice but is meant to present a message of the government to the population. Dictatorships use show trials to destroy opponents and to frighten people.
wichtigste: In a show trial, the verdict has been decided before the proceedings.
It is staged in public, often with newspapers, radio or television.
The defendants are often forced into confessions with threats or torture.
The Moscow Trials under Joseph Stalin from 1936 to 1938 are famous.
Under National Socialism, the People's Court held show trials, for example against the White Rose.
Under the rule of law, independent courts and fair proceedings prevent such trials.
Show trials are meant to deter people and make the government look right.

abschnitte.text: A **show trial** looks like a normal court case, but in reality it is a piece of theatre. The judges, the prosecutors and often even the defence lawyers work in the government's interest. The **verdict** has already been decided by those in power. The word “show” makes it clear that it is mainly about the effect on the audience.

Before the trial, the defendants are often interrogated, threatened or tortured for weeks. Many then make a **confession** that is not true at all, sometimes to protect their family. In the courtroom they repeat the sentences they have learned by heart. Newspapers and radio report in detail so that as many people as possible hear about it.

Show trials are meant to show that the government is supposedly in the right and that its opponents are traitors. They are meant to make the population **afraid**, so that nobody resists. Opponents are often blamed for problems that are actually the government's fault. In this way attention is drawn away from the government's own mistakes.

In the Soviet Union, **Joseph Stalin** had the **Moscow Trials** held from 1936 to 1938, at which former comrades such as Nikolai Bukharin were sentenced to death. Under National Socialism, the **People's Court** under Roland Freisler sentenced Sophie and Hans Scholl of the White Rose resistance group to death in 1943. There were also such trials after the attempt on Hitler's life on 20 July 1944. In Czechoslovakia, the Slánský trial of leading communists took place in 1952.

Under the **rule of law**, the presumption of innocence applies, and the court only decides after examining all the evidence. Judges are independent and may not be influenced by the government. Defendants have the right to their own lawyer and do not have to incriminate themselves. Forced confessions may not be used.

begriffe.erklaerung: When someone admits to having committed an act.
A person who is accused of a crime in court.
A special court under National Socialism that convicted political opponents.
Everyone is considered innocent until their guilt is proven.

gewusst: The trials of the men of 20 July 1944 were filmed, but the recordings were never shown in public as planned.
Many victims of show trials were officially rehabilitated decades later, meaning declared innocent.

teile.einleitung: Stolpersteine are small memorial plaques set into the ground. They remember people who were persecuted, driven out or murdered during the time of National Socialism.
wichtigste: The Cologne artist Gunter Demnig started the project.
A Stolperstein is a concrete cube with a brass plate.
It lies in front of a victim's last freely chosen home.
Many inscriptions begin with “Hier wohnte” (Here lived).
The 100,000th stone was laid in Nuremberg in 2023.
Switzerland's first Stolpersteine have been in Kreuzlingen since 2013.

abschnitte.text: The Cologne artist **Gunter Demnig** started the project in the 1990s. He wanted the victims of **National Socialism** to become visible where they had lived. He lays many of the stones himself. Often neighbours, school classes or relatives order a stone and research the person's life story beforehand.

A Stolperstein is a small **concrete cube**. On top there is a **brass plate** into which the name and dates of the person's life are stamped. The stone is set level into the **pavement**. It lies in front of the victim's last freely chosen **home**. That is why many inscriptions begin with “Hier wohnte” (Here lived). For many victims at one place there are **Stolperschwellen** (stumbling thresholds), brass plates about one metre long.

In May 2023 Gunter Demnig laid the **100,000th stone** in **Nuremberg**. There are Stolpersteine in many countries of Europe. The project is regarded as the **largest decentralised memorial** in the world. Decentralised means that it does not stand in one place but is spread across many towns and villages.

On **8 September 2013**, the first two Stolpersteine in Switzerland were laid in **Kreuzlingen** in the canton of **Thurgau**. Later other places followed, such as **Zurich**, **Basel**, **Bern** and **St Gallen**. They remember people with a connection to Switzerland who were persecuted, for example because they were turned away at the border.

Not everyone likes Stolpersteine. Some think it is undignified to walk on the names of victims. In 2015 the city council of **Munich** decided not to allow Stolpersteine on public ground. Instead the city uses its own memorial signs on the walls of buildings. Stolpersteine are allowed there on private ground.

gewusst: Anyone reading a Stolperstein has to bow slightly; Gunter Demnig intended it that way.
Because walking keeps the brass plate polished, Stolpersteine that many people walk over shine especially brightly.

teile.einleitung: A constitutional court is a court that makes sure the constitution is respected. It checks whether laws and the actions of the government are in line with the constitution. Dictators like to abolish such courts or fill them with their own people.
wichtigste: A constitutional court checks whether laws and government actions comply with the constitution.
It can declare laws invalid if they violate fundamental rights.
To do its job, it must be independent of the government and parliament.
The world's first special constitutional court was set up in Austria in 1920.
In Germany the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe is very well known.
Switzerland has no separate constitutional court for federal laws.
In dictatorships, constitutional courts are stripped of their power or filled with loyal supporters.

abschnitte.text: A **constitutional court** is a special court that deals with the most important rules of a state. It decides whether a law is compatible with the constitution. If it is not, the court can strike down the law. That is why it is also called the “guardian of the constitution”.

In many countries, anyone who feels their **fundamental rights** have been violated can turn to the constitutional court. In Germany this is called a constitutional complaint. The judges examine the case carefully and give written reasons for their ruling. Governments, parliaments or federal states can also call on the court when they are in dispute with each other.

In 1920 Austria founded the first **Constitutional Court**; the idea came from the legal scholar Hans Kelsen. The German **Federal Constitutional Court** in Karlsruhe began its work in 1951. In the USA, the Supreme Court takes on this task, and has done so since a famous ruling in 1803. Its decisions, for example on ending racial segregation in schools in 1954, have shaped the country's history.

Switzerland has no constitutional court that may strike down federal laws. The **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne has to apply federal laws, even if they might contradict the constitution. The reason is that in Switzerland the people should have the final say, because they can call a referendum against laws. The Federal Supreme Court can, however, check cantonal laws to see whether they are constitutional.

An independent constitutional court is inconvenient for dictators because it limits their power. That is why authoritarian governments often try to weaken the courts. They appoint their own supporters as judges, shorten terms of office or take powers away from the court. Experts see such attacks on the **independence of the judiciary** as a warning sign that democracy is in danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: A legal action with which a person defends themselves against a violation of their fundamental rights.
Judges may not accept orders from the government or parties.
The highest court in Switzerland, based in Lausanne.
Checking whether a law is in line with the constitution.

gewusst: The judges at the German Federal Constitutional Court wear red robes.
A 1803 ruling of the US Supreme Court established that courts may check laws for constitutionality at all, even though the constitution does not say so.
The Swiss parliament has discussed a constitutional court several times but has always rejected it so far.

teile.einleitung: Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo is President of Equatorial Guinea, a small country in Central Africa. He has been in power since 1979 and is one of the longest-serving heads of state in the world (as of 2026).
wichtigste: Obiang has ruled Equatorial Guinea since August 1979.
He came to power through a coup against his own uncle.
Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa with Spanish as an official language.
Since the 1990s, oil has brought a lot of money into the country.
His son Teodorín is vice-president (as of 2026).
In 2016 Geneva seized luxury cars belonging to Teodorín.

abschnitte.text: **Equatorial Guinea** is in Central Africa on the **Gulf of Guinea**. It was a **Spanish colony**. That is why it is the only country in Africa with **Spanish** as an official language. French and Portuguese are also official languages. The country is small and has only a few inhabitants.

The first dictator after independence was **Francisco Macías Nguema**, Obiang's **uncle**. His rule was very brutal. In August 1979 Obiang overthrew him in a **coup**. Macías Nguema was sentenced to death and executed. Since then Obiang has ruled the country.

**Oil** has been produced in Equatorial Guinea since the 1990s. Since then the country has been one of the richest in Africa per person. Even so, a large part of the population lives in **poverty**. Critics say that it is mainly the **ruling family** and the people around them who profit from the oil.

Obiang's son **Teodorín Nguema Obiang Mangue** is vice-president (as of 2026). Critics see this as an attempt to keep power in the family. In 2016 the **Geneva public prosecutor's office** seized several expensive sports cars belonging to Teodorín. In 2019, 25 of his cars were auctioned. They raised around **27 million francs**.

gewusst: In 2015 Equatorial Guinea stepped in at short notice as host of the Africa Cup of Nations.
The country had already hosted the Africa Cup of Nations together with Gabon in 2012.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of assembly means that people may meet peacefully to discuss something, make decisions or show an opinion together. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution protects this right. In dictatorships, on the other hand, meetings of critics are often forbidden.
wichtigste: Freedom of assembly means that you may meet peacefully with others.
The Federal Constitution protects peaceful gatherings, including protests.
Thanks to freedom of association, you may set up clubs and associations in Switzerland.
At the annual general meeting, the members of a club meet.
At the municipal assembly, the voters decide about matters in the village.
At the Landsgemeinde, people show by raising their hand whether they agree.
Dictatorships often ban meetings of opponents of the government.

abschnitte.text: People meet to discuss or show something together. **Freedom of assembly** protects this right as long as the gathering is **peaceful**. In Switzerland it is written in the **Federal Constitution**. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights also mentions this right. Without freedom of assembly, people could hardly show their opinions together.

Closely related is **freedom of association**. It allows people to set up clubs and associations, for example a football club, a choir or a nature conservation society. There are a great many clubs in Switzerland. Once a year the members meet for the **annual general meeting**. There they elect the committee, look at the accounts and decide together on important questions.

abschnitte.titel: Assemblies in the municipality and canton
abschnitte.text: Many Swiss municipalities have a **municipal assembly**. There the voters decide, for example, on a new school building or the budget. The cantons of **Glarus** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden** still have the **Landsgemeinde**. The voters meet in the open air and raise their hand or their voting card. That way you can see how many are in favour.

In Switzerland you may also hold a **demonstration** to protest against something. It is important that it stays peaceful. Rallies on public streets and squares usually need **permission** from the municipality or town. The authorities then decide, for example, where the march goes. This is meant to protect the rights of the demonstrators and of other people.

In dictatorships, freedom of assembly is often severely restricted. **Opponents of the government** in particular are often not allowed to meet. Those in power are afraid that people will join forces against them. Anyone who demonstrates anyway risks arrest. That is why freedom of assembly is seen as an important feature of a **democracy**.

gewusst: The Landsgemeinde in Glarus is one of the oldest forms of direct democracy.
In Appenzell Innerrhoden, men used to be allowed to bring a side arm to the Landsgemeinde as proof of their right to vote.

teile.einleitung: “Volksgemeinschaft” (national community) was a central term of National Socialist propaganda. It promised unity among all Germans across classes and parties. At the same time it excluded many people and served to persecute them.
wichtigste: With the Volksgemeinschaft, Nazi propaganda promised unity across all classes.
It built on the “spirit of 1914” at the beginning of the First World War.
Jews, political opponents and other groups were excluded as “alien to the community”.
The slogan “You are nothing, your people is everything” placed the individual below the community.
“Strength through Joy” offered workers cheap trips, theatre and sport.
The cheap Volksempfänger radio brought propaganda into many households.
From 1935, the Reich Labour Service was compulsory for young men.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the **First World War** in 1914, many Germans spoke of a unity across all classes and parties. The National Socialists built on this **“spirit of 1914”**. They promised a **Volksgemeinschaft** in which all “national comrades” would stick together. The slogan **“You are nothing, your people is everything”** shows what it was about: the individual person only counted as part of the people. Personal rights had to take second place.

Not everyone belonged to the Volksgemeinschaft. Jews, political opponents and other groups were regarded as **“alien to the community”**. They were excluded, deprived of their rights and persecuted. Unity on the inside and **exclusion** on the outside belonged inseparably together. That is why historians today see the term as a tool of the dictatorship.

The organisation **“Kraft durch Freude”** (Strength through Joy) was part of the German Labour Front. It offered workers cheap holiday trips, theatre visits and sport, even cruises. This was meant to win the workers over to the regime. A savings scheme promised the **KdF-Wagen**, a car for everyone. Hundreds of thousands paid in, but during the war the factory built military vehicles, and no saver received their car.

The **Volksempfänger** (people's receiver) was introduced in 1933 and was much cheaper than other radios. In this way propaganda could reach as many households as possible. On **Eintopfsonntag** (stew Sunday), families were supposed to cook only a simple meal and donate the money saved to the **Winter Relief**. This also put social pressure on people. From **1935**, young men had to work for six months in the **Reich Labour Service**, for example building roads or in agriculture.

After the Second World War, the idea of the Volksgemeinschaft was closely studied. It shows how a dictatorship tried to win approval with offers and a feeling of community. At the same time it served to exclude people. That is why the term is regarded as tainted today. In democracies like Switzerland, the **rights of the individual** are protected in the constitution.

gewusst: The Volksempfänger was called VE 301; the number recalled 30 January 1933, the day the Nazis took power.
After the war, the KdF-Wagen became the VW Beetle.

t1m7tuwp.t: Coming to terms with the past

teile.einleitung: Coming to terms with the past, in German “Vergangenheitsbewältigung”, means dealing with injustice that happened in a dictatorship or a war. A society looks back honestly, names the perpetrators and remembers the victims. This is meant to prevent such injustice from happening again.
wichtigste: Coming to terms with the past means society dealing with injustice that has been committed.
It includes trials, investigations, compensation and memorials.
After the Second World War, leading National Socialists were convicted at the Nuremberg trials.
After the end of the GDR, people were able to see their Stasi files.
After apartheid, South Africa set up a truth commission.
Switzerland has also investigated its role in the Second World War and the fate of the Verdingkinder.
Remembering is important so that young people can learn from history.

abschnitte.text: After a **dictatorship** ends, many questions remain: who was responsible, what exactly happened and how can the victims get justice? **Dealing with the past** tries to answer these questions honestly. This is often painful, because some perpetrators are still alive and many people would rather forget. Even so, it is seen as important for a healthy democracy.

One way of dealing with the past is **trials** of those responsible. From 1945 to 1946, leading National Socialists stood before an international court at the Nuremberg trials. Later, guards from the Auschwitz concentration camp were also charged in Germany, for example in the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials from 1963. Today there is the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which prosecutes serious crimes.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germany opened the files of the GDR secret police, the **Stasi**, in 1992. Many people found out from them that friends or neighbours had spied on them. In South Africa, after the end of apartheid, a **truth commission** under Archbishop Desmond Tutu worked from 1996. Perpetrators could confess their deeds in public, and victims were given the chance to tell their stories.

Memorials, museums and monuments keep memories alive. In Berlin, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe has stood since 2005. In many cities there are small brass stones in the ground, the **Stolpersteine**, with the names of victims of National Socialism. The artist Gunter Demnig has laid tens of thousands of them, including in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Dealing with the past in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Switzerland was not a dictatorship, but it has also dealt with chapters of its own past. From 1996 to 2001 the **Bergier Commission** investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War, for example its refugee policy and its business with Nazi Germany. Later the injustice done to **Verdingkinder** (contract children) and other victims of compulsory social measures was recognised. Since 2016 those affected have been able to receive a solidarity payment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Carefully investigating and discussing injustice from the past.
A group that investigates the crimes of a former regime and makes them public.
A small memorial stone in the ground in front of the last home of a victim of the Nazis.
A child in Switzerland in the past who was taken away from their parents and made to work for other families.

gewusst: Placed in a row, the Stasi files would be many kilometres long.
The term “Vergangenheitsbewältigung” was coined in German and is sometimes used untranslated in other languages too.
27 January, the day of the liberation of Auschwitz in 1945, is now an international day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Greece, tyranny was the sole rule of a man who had not inherited power but had seized it himself. Only later did the word “tyrant” come to mean a cruel, violent ruler.
wichtigste: A tyrant usually came to power through force or popular support, not through inheritance.
Peisistratos was the best-known tyrant of Athens.
Harmodius and Aristogeiton were honoured as the “Tyrannicides”.
Ostracism was meant to prevent new tyrants.
Polycrates of Samos is known from Schiller's ballad.
Solon refused to become a tyrant.

abschnitte.text: In ancient Greece, a **tyrant** was originally a sole ruler **without a hereditary right** to rule. He usually came to power through force or through the favour of the people. Some tyrants promoted building, trade and the arts. In **Corinth**, in the 7th century BC, **Cypselus** overthrew the noble family of the Bacchiadae. His son **Periander** succeeded him. That is why the family is called the **Cypselids**.

The lawgiver **Solon** carried out reforms around 594 BC. He could have taken sole power but chose not to. Later **Peisistratos** seized power several times and ruled until his death in 527 BC. He promoted buildings, cults and festivals such as the **Panathenaea**. In 514 BC **Harmodius and Aristogeiton** murdered Hipparchus, the brother of the tyrant Hippias. The tyranny only ended in 510 BC, but the two were still honoured with statues.

Under **Cleisthenes**, Athens introduced **ostracism**, the “potsherd court”. With it the citizens could banish a politician who had become too powerful for **ten years**. The names were scratched onto **pieces of broken pottery**. This was meant to stop a tyranny from returning.

According to Herodotus, **Polycrates** of Samos threw a valuable ring into the sea to reduce his great good fortune. But he found it again in the belly of a fish. **Friedrich Schiller** turned the story into the ballad “The Ring of Polycrates” in 1797. The story of the **Sword of Damocles** is set at the court of **Dionysius** in Syracuse. Dionysius had a sword hung by a horsehair above Damocles to show how threatened a ruler is.

gewusst: The phrase “Sword of Damocles” is still used today for a constant threat.
In some traditions, Periander of Corinth is counted among the Seven Sages.

teile.einleitung: The Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought is the most important human rights prize of the European Union. Every year since 1988, the European Parliament has awarded it to people or groups who stand up for freedom and human rights.
wichtigste: The European Parliament has awarded the prize since 1988.
It is named after the Soviet physicist and dissident Andrei Sakharov.
The prize is worth 50,000 euros.
The first winners were Nelson Mandela and Anatoly Marchenko.
In 2022 it went to the Ukrainian people, and in 2023 to Jina Mahsa Amini and the Iranian protest movement.

abschnitte.text: **Andrei Sakharov** was an important **nuclear physicist** in the Soviet Union. Later he bravely stood up for **human rights** and freedom of expression. For this he was persecuted by the government and banished to the city of Gorky. In 1975 he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The European Parliament's prize honours his memory.

Every year the **European Parliament** chooses the prize-winners. The award ceremony usually takes place in December in **Strasbourg**. The prize is worth **50,000 euros**. Often the worldwide **attention** is more important than the money. It can protect people in danger and make their causes known.

In 1988 the prize went to **Nelson Mandela** from South Africa, who was still in prison at the time. He shared it with the Soviet dissident **Anatoly Marchenko**, who had died in prison in 1986. Later many other well-known people were honoured, for example the young Pakistani **Malala Yousafzai** in 2013.

In 2022 the Parliament honoured the **Ukrainian people** for their resistance to Russia's war of aggression. In 2023 **Jina Mahsa Amini** and the Iranian movement **“Woman, Life, Freedom”** received the prize. In 2024 it went to the Venezuelan opposition politicians **María Corina Machado** and **Edmundo González** for their efforts for free elections.

gewusst: Some prize-winners could not collect the prize themselves because they were in prison or were not allowed to leave their country.
Andrei Sakharov is regarded as one of the fathers of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, before he began to work for peace and human rights.

teile.einleitung: State media are newspapers, broadcasters and news agencies that are controlled by the state. In dictatorships they spread what the government wants and are its mouthpiece.
wichtigste: State media in dictatorships may not criticise the government.
The Soviet party newspaper was called “Pravda”, which means “truth”.
In the GDR, “Neues Deutschland” was the newspaper of the SED.
North Korea's news agency is called KCNA, and China's is called Xinhua.
In 2022 the EU banned the Russian state broadcaster RT.
Reporters Without Borders rates press freedom every year.

abschnitte.text: Free media report independently and may criticise the government. **State media** in a dictatorship, on the other hand, are controlled by the government. Critical reports are not allowed there. The media are meant to win people over to the policies of those in power. This is called **propaganda**.

**“Pravda”** was the newspaper of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Its name means **“truth”**, yet it mainly spread propaganda. In the GDR, **“Neues Deutschland”** (New Germany) was the central organ of the SED. The newspaper printed what the party leadership dictated. The National Socialists had already had the cheap **Volksempfänger VE 301** radio built. The number recalls 30 January 1933, the day Hitler became Reich Chancellor.

The **Korean Central News Agency (KCNA)** spreads the reports of the North Korean leadership. There are no independent media in North Korea. China's state agency is called **Xinhua**, which means “New China”. After the Russian attack on Ukraine, the EU banned the state broadcasters **RT** and **Sputnik** in March 2022. It justified this with deliberate disinformation.

From 1960 to 1989, GDR television broadcast **“Der schwarze Kanal”** (The Black Channel). The presenter **Karl-Eduard von Schnitzler** showed clips from Western television. He twisted their meaning to fit SED propaganda and made disparaging comments about them. In this way Western television was meant to look like lies.

The organisation **Reporters Without Borders**, based in Paris, compares 180 states every year. Countries with powerful state media and censorship end up far down the list. In Switzerland, the **Federal Constitution** guarantees the independence of radio and television. The **SRG** is financed by licence fees, but the government may not tell it what to report.

gewusst: The newspaper “Pravda” was called “truth”, and yet it was a tool of propaganda.
The Volksempfänger was especially cheap so that as many households as possible could listen to Nazi propaganda.

teile.einleitung: Saudi Arabia is the largest country on the Arabian Peninsula. It is an absolute monarchy: the king holds the highest power, and there is no elected parliament and no permitted parties.
wichtigste: Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy.
The state was founded in 1932 by Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud and bears the name of his family.
Salman bin Abd al-Aziz has been king since 2015.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, MBS for short, is regarded as the real ruler.
Political parties are banned.
Since 2018 women have been allowed to drive.

abschnitte.text: In Saudi Arabia, the **king** holds the highest power in government, law-making and the courts. There is no elected parliament, and **political parties** are banned. The **Shura**, an advisory assembly, is appointed by the king. It may give advice but cannot pass laws on its own. The legal system is based on a strict interpretation of **Islam**.

The state was founded in **1932** by **Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud**. It bears the name of his family, the **Al Saud**. Since then his sons have ruled one after another. **King Salman** has been in power since **2015**. His son **Mohammed bin Salman**, often called **MBS**, is crown prince and prime minister and is regarded as the real ruler.

Saudi Arabia has huge **oil reserves** and is one of the largest oil-producing countries in the world. The oil has made the country very rich. **Mecca** and **Medina**, the holiest cities of Islam, are also in the country. Every year millions of believers come to Mecca on pilgrimage. The capital is called **Riyadh**.

For a long time Saudi Arabia was the only country where women were not allowed to **drive**. In June **2018** the ban was lifted. Today women may also go to concerts and football matches. The crown prince wants to modernise the country and make it less dependent on oil. But there are still hardly any political freedoms.

Anyone who criticises the leadership risks harsh punishment. In 2014 the blogger **Raif Badawi** was sentenced to ten years in prison and 1000 lashes because of his writings. In 2018 the journalist **Jamal Khashoggi** was murdered in the Saudi consulate in **Istanbul**. Both cases caused outrage all over the world.

gewusst: Saudi Arabia has no rivers that carry water all year round.
A large part of the country is desert, including the Rub' al Khali, one of the largest sand deserts in the world.

teile.einleitung: In 2020 Russia's constitution was changed considerably. The changes concerned the power of the president, the relationship with international law and social values. The rule that Vladimir Putin's previous terms of office no longer count received particular attention.
wichtigste: Vladimir Putin announced the constitutional amendment in January 2020.
On the same day, Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev resigned with the whole government.
The vote lasted a week and ended on 1 July 2020.
Officially around 78 per cent voted in favour; independent observers criticised many irregularities.
Putin's previous terms were reset to zero, so he could remain president until 2036.
Since then the Russian constitution has taken priority over conflicting international decisions.
The constitution defines marriage as a union of a man and a woman.

abschnitte.text: In **January 2020**, President Vladimir Putin proposed in a speech that the constitution be changed. Shortly afterwards Prime Minister **Dmitry Medvedev** resigned with the whole government. The new prime minister was **Mikhail Mishustin**. The proposals then went through parliament. Later a change was added that became especially well known: resetting Putin's terms of office to zero.

The vote was originally planned for the spring. Because of the **Covid pandemic**, it was postponed. In the end it lasted a week and ended on **1 July 2020**. According to the official result, around **78 per cent** voted in favour. However, independent observers and opposition figures criticised many **irregularities**, for example in how voting was checked.

In Russia a president may only serve two terms in a row. Since 2012 a term has lasted **six years**. With the change, Putin's earlier terms no longer count. Critics call this **resetting to zero**. This allowed Putin to stand again in 2024 and 2030. In 2024 he was re-elected, and with a further term he could remain in office until **2036**.

Since 2020 the constitution has stated that it takes **priority**. Decisions of international bodies that contradict the Russian constitution do not have to be implemented in Russia. This concerns, for example, rulings by international courts. Supporters saw this as protecting the country's own independence. Critics said that citizens would lose protection against decisions of their own state.

Social values were also written into the constitution. For example, **marriage** is defined only as a union of a man and a woman. It also states that pensions should be adjusted regularly. The protection of the Russian language was also stressed. Altogether, a great many articles of the 1993 constitution were changed. Supporters and opponents still judge these changes very differently today.

gewusst: Resetting the terms to zero was proposed in parliament by Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space.
The 2020 vote took place over several days so that not too many people would meet at the same time because of Covid.

teile.einleitung: The SS, the Schutzstaffel (protection squad), was an organisation of the National Socialists in Germany. It began as a small bodyguard unit for Hitler and became the most powerful and most feared organisation in the Nazi state. It bore the main responsibility for the Holocaust.
wichtigste: SS is short for Schutzstaffel.
The SS was formed in 1925 as a bodyguard unit for Hitler.
From 1929, Heinrich Himmler led the SS as “Reichsführer SS”.
From 1932 the SS wore black uniforms.
In 1934 it eliminated the leadership of the SA.
The SS ran and guarded the concentration camps.

abschnitte.text: The **SS** was formed in **1925** as a small unit meant to protect **Adolf Hitler** at events. At first it was in the shadow of the much larger **SA**, the NSDAP's storm troopers. From **1929** **Heinrich Himmler** was “Reichsführer SS”. He built the SS up into a huge **power machine**.

At first the SS wore the brown shirt of the SA with a black cap and tie. From **1932** it was given a **black uniform**. In this way it wanted to set itself apart from the SA as an **elite**. Its members were to be unconditionally loyal to Hitler. The symbols of the SS were the skull and two runes.

At the end of **June 1934**, Hitler had the leadership of the **SA** murdered by the SS. The National Socialists called this the “Röhm Putsch”. After that the SS was independent and gained more and more power. Later it also controlled the **police** and the secret police, the **Gestapo**. The SS watched and persecuted everyone who was regarded as an opponent.

The SS ran and guarded the **concentration camps**. There were special units for this, the **Death's Head units**. In the Second World War the SS organised the **Holocaust**, the murder of around six million Jews. Many other people were also persecuted and killed. Himmler was one of those mainly responsible.

As well as the general SS, there was the **Waffen-SS**, which was used as a fighting force in the war. After the war, the court at the **Nuremberg trials** declared the SS a **criminal organisation**. Himmler took his own life after his capture in 1945. Many SS perpetrators were convicted, but many others were never punished.

gewusst: Its symbols, the double rune and the skull, are banned in Germany today.
Towards the end of the war the SS had hundreds of thousands of members.

teile.einleitung: Sanctions are punitive measures against states or individuals who, for example, violate human rights or attack other countries. They are meant to put on pressure without waging war. Switzerland also applies sanctions.
wichtigste: Sanctions are punitive measures without weapons.
Targeted sanctions hit individual rulers instead of a whole people.
Frozen assets are blocked but still belong to the owner.
The UN Security Council can pass sanctions that are binding on all member states.
In Switzerland, sanctions are based on the Embargo Act.
SECO applies them, and Switzerland often adopts EU sanctions.

abschnitte.text: With **sanctions**, states want to make a government change its behaviour. In the past, whole countries were often targeted, for example with a trade ban. But it was mainly the population that suffered. Today **targeted sanctions** are often used. They only hit certain rulers and their supporters.

A common measure is **freezing assets**. The person affected can then no longer use their money, accounts or goods. But they are not taken away. With an **entry ban**, someone may no longer enter a country, for example to go shopping or on holiday. There are also **arms embargoes**, meaning bans on supplying weapons.

The **UN Security Council** can pass sanctions that all member states have to follow. Each of the five permanent members, namely the USA, Russia, China, Great Britain and France, can block this with a **veto**. That is why individual states or groups such as the **EU** also pass their own sanctions.

In Switzerland, sanctions are based on the **Embargo Act**. It allows the **Federal Council** to adopt sanctions of the UN or of important trading partners. They are applied by the **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs**, **SECO**. Switzerland is not in the EU but often adopts its sanctions, for example those against Russia from February 2022.

The Russian auditor **Sergei Magnitsky** uncovered a large tax fraud and died in Russian custody in 2009. In 2012 the **USA** passed a law named after him. It allows sanctions against individual **human rights violators**. Later other states introduced similar rules.

gewusst: Switzerland has already returned money of overthrown rulers to their countries, for example Ferdinand Marcos's money to the Philippines.
Sanctions lists often contain thousands of names of people and companies.

teile.einleitung: The Blackshirts were the fighting squads of the Italian fascists. They helped Benito Mussolini to power with violence and intimidation and later became part of the state.
wichtigste: The fascist fighting squads in Italy wore black shirts.
The squads were called “squadre”, and their members “squadristi”.
They attacked mainly socialists, trade unionists and farmers' associations.
They took their clothing from the Arditi, assault troops from the First World War.
In 1923 they were made part of a state militia.
In 1924 fascists murdered the socialist member of parliament Giacomo Matteotti.

abschnitte.text: After the **First World War**, Italy was marked by poverty, unemployment and fierce conflict between political camps. Many former soldiers could not find their way in civilian life. The **Arditi** in particular, Italian assault troops, had already worn black shirts during the war. Many of them joined **Benito Mussolini**'s fascist movement. This is how the black shirt became their mark of recognition.

The squads were called **squadre** in Italian, and their members **squadristi**. They raided the offices of trade unions, newspapers and parties and beat opponents with wooden clubs, the **manganello**. They often forced people to drink large amounts of **castor oil**, a strong laxative. This was meant to humiliate them and was dangerous. With acts like these, the Blackshirts spread fear.

In October 1922, thousands of Blackshirts moved towards the capital in the so-called **March on Rome**. The king gave in and appointed Mussolini prime minister. In 1923 the fighting squads were made part of the **Milizia Volontaria per la Sicurezza Nazionale**, the Voluntary Militia for National Security. In this way a party force became part of the state.

In 1924 the socialist member of parliament **Giacomo Matteotti** denounced electoral fraud and fascist violence in parliament. Shortly afterwards he was kidnapped and murdered by fascist thugs. The crime caused great outrage. Mussolini survived the crisis and afterwards expanded his **dictatorship** further.

The Blackshirts became a model for similar groups in other countries. In Germany, the NSDAP's **Sturmabteilung (SA)** wore brown shirts and was therefore called the **Brownshirts**. It too used violence against political opponents. In the 1920s and 1930s, coloured shirts became the mark of many fascist movements.

gewusst: In Italy, the word “Blackshirt” became a term for a convinced fascist.
The club, “manganello” in Italian, became a symbol of the violence of the squadristi.

teile.einleitung: A troll farm is an organisation in which people are paid to spread comments and posts on the internet in a targeted way. They often use fake accounts to do this and want to influence public opinion.
wichtigste: The best-known troll farm is the Internet Research Agency in St Petersburg.
In 2023 Yevgeny Prigozhin admitted that he had founded it.
It is said to have tried to influence the 2016 US presidential election.
In China there are state-directed commentators known as the “50 Cent Party”.
In astroturfing, a citizens' movement is only faked.

abschnitte.text: The **Internet Research Agency** in **St Petersburg** became known from around 2013. Hundreds of employees spread comments and posts using fake accounts. In 2015 the journalist **Lyudmila Savchuk** got herself hired undercover. She reported on shift work, daily targets and fake profiles. The businessman **Yevgeny Prigozhin**, later head of the **Wagner** mercenary group, admitted in February 2023 that he had founded the company. He was killed in a plane crash in August 2023.

In February 2018 the US special counsel **Robert Mueller** charged 13 Russian individuals and three organisations. They are said to have tried to influence the **2016 US presidential election**. Using fake accounts on social media, they allegedly stirred up feelings and fuelled conflict. Troll farms often aim to divide a society.

In China, state-directed commentators are mockingly called the **50 Cent Party**, **“Wumao”** in Chinese. The name refers to the rumour that they are paid 50 fen per post. In 2017 a study led by the Harvard political scientist **Gary King** estimated around **448 million** fake posts per year. They mostly do not argue with critics but **distract** and push sensitive topics aside with cheerful posts.

**Astroturfing** means faking a broad citizens' movement. The name comes from the artificial grass brand **“AstroTurf”**: instead of a real “grassroots movement”, an artificial one is created. Signs of it are many new accounts that post almost identical texts at the same time. So when you read things on the internet, you should check who is behind an opinion.

gewusst: In the troll farm in St Petersburg there were fixed daily targets for the number of posts.
According to the 2017 study, the directed posts in China were written mainly by government employees.

teile.einleitung: The Somoza dynasty ruled Nicaragua from 1936 to 1979. A father and his two sons passed power on within the family, relying on the National Guard.
wichtigste: Anastasio Somoza García was head of the National Guard from 1933.
In 1934 he had the rebel Augusto César Sandino murdered.
In 1936 he came to power through a coup.
In 1956 he was shot by the poet Rigoberto López Pérez.
His sons Luis and Anastasio Somoza Debayle succeeded him.
In 1979 the family was overthrown after about 43 years in power.

abschnitte.text: The **National Guard** was built up under US occupation. In 1933 **Anastasio Somoza García** became its head. The rebel **Augusto César Sandino** had fought against the US troops. In 1934, after peace talks, he was shot by members of the National Guard on Somoza's orders. In 1936 Somoza García took power himself through a **coup**.

In 1956 the young poet **Rigoberto López Pérez** shot Somoza García in **León**. The attacker was killed immediately, and Somoza died a few days later. His son **Luis Somoza Debayle** became president and remained so until 1963. The younger brother **Anastasio Somoza Debayle** led the National Guard at the same time and later became president himself. He had graduated from the US military academy **West Point** in 1946.

During the **Cold War**, the Somozas were seen as close allies of the USA. They presented themselves as opponents of communism. In June 1979 a National Guardsman shot the ABC reporter **Bill Stewart** while his camera team was filming. The pictures were shown on US television. They greatly weakened support for Somoza in the USA.

The Sandinistas, named after Sandino, led an uprising against the regime. On 17 July 1979, Anastasio Somoza Debayle flew to **Miami**. However, he was not allowed to stay in the USA permanently and moved on to **Paraguay**. Counting from 1936 to 1979, the family ruled Nicaragua for about **43 years**.

gewusst: In 1956 a poet killed the founder of the Somoza dynasty.
The last Somoza was a graduate of the famous West Point military academy.
