teile.einleitung: The UN Convention against Torture is an international treaty against torture. It bans torture without exception and obliges states to prevent and punish it.
wichtigste: The convention came into force on 26 June 1987.
Torture in the sense of the convention comes from the state or is approved by it.
The ban also applies in war and in a state of emergency.
Nobody may be deported to a country where they face torture.
A committee of ten experts in Geneva monitors compliance.
An additional protocol from 2002 allows visits to places of detention.

abschnitte.text: The **United Nations** Convention against Torture came into force on **26 June 1987**. That is why this day is now the **International Day in Support of Victims of Torture**. Many states have signed the treaty, including **Switzerland**. By doing so they commit themselves to preventing torture and punishing those who commit it.

**Article 1** describes torture as deliberately causing severe pain by a **public official** or with their consent. So the convention is directed against **state violence**, for example by the police or prison staff. **Article 2** states that no exceptional circumstances justify torture. Neither war nor a state of emergency nor an order from a superior is an excuse.

**Article 3** contains the principle of **non-refoulement**. Nobody may be extradited or deported to a country where they face a serious risk of torture. This principle also plays an important role in asylum decisions in Switzerland.

The **Committee against Torture (CAT)** has **ten** independent members and meets in **Geneva**. The states that have signed the treaty must submit reports to it regularly. The **Optional Protocol (OPCAT)** of 2002 creates a UN subcommittee. It obliges states to set up national bodies that may visit prisons, police stations and psychiatric hospitals without notice. In Switzerland this is done by the **National Commission for the Prevention of Torture**.

In 1998 the former Chilean dictator **Augusto Pinochet** was arrested in **London**. Spain demanded his extradition for torture crimes. The Law Lords of the British House of Lords ruled that extradition was permissible. They based this on the Convention against Torture. The case showed that even former heads of state can be held responsible for torture.

gewusst: The ban on torture is one of the few rules in international law that applies absolutely.
The UN Committee against Torture is based in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Suharto was President of Indonesia from 1967 to 1998. He ruled in an authoritarian way for more than 30 years and called his rule the “New Order”.
wichtigste: Suharto ruled Indonesia from 1967 to 1998.
After 1965 he pushed aside the first president, Sukarno.
His rise was accompanied by mass killings of supposed communists.
In 1975 he had East Timor occupied.
The Asian financial crisis led to his resignation in 1998.
His successor was B. J. Habibie.

abschnitte.text: **Sukarno** was the first president of Indonesia after independence. In 1965 there was a failed **coup attempt**. After that, the army under General **Suharto** hunted down real and supposed **communists**. Estimates range from 500,000 to one million deaths. Suharto pushed Sukarno out of power step by step and became president in 1967.

Suharto called his time in government the **“New Order”**, **“Orde Baru”** in Indonesian. In this way he set himself apart from Sukarno. The economy grew, but criticism was hardly allowed. Under the principle of **“Dwifungsi”**, the dual function, the **army** had political tasks as well as defence. Officers sat in parliament and in ministries.
In 1975 Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of **East Timor**. The occupation lasted more than two decades and cost many people their lives. East Timor only became independent in **2002**.

In 1997 and 1998 the **Asian financial crisis** hit Indonesia hard. The currency crashed, and prices rose sharply. In the capital **Jakarta** on the island of **Java** there were large protests. In May 1998 Suharto resigned. Vice-President **Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie** took over. Under him, democratisation began, known as **“Reformasi”**.

gewusst: Like many people on Java, Suharto had only one name, and so did his predecessor Sukarno.
Indonesia is the country with the most islands in the world.

teile.einleitung: Civil disobedience means deliberately breaking a rule without violence in order to draw attention to an injustice. Famous examples are Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King in the USA. There have also been well-known actions in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Civil disobedience is a deliberate, non-violent breaking of rules for reasons of conscience.
Henry David Thoreau wrote a famous essay on it in 1849.
In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama.
In 1963 Martin Luther King wrote a letter from Birmingham jail.
Anyone who practises civil disobedience knowingly accepts the punishment.
In 1975 opponents of nuclear power occupied the building site of the Kaiseraugst nuclear power station.

abschnitte.text: In **civil disobedience**, you break a rule **publicly** and **without violence**. The aim is to draw attention to an injustice. According to the classic view, you **knowingly accept the punishment**. In this way you show how seriously you take the cause. A permitted **demonstration**, on the other hand, is legal and is not civil disobedience.

The American writer **Henry David Thoreau** refused to pay taxes. The money helped to pay for slavery and a war. As a result he spent a night in prison. In **1849** he wrote an essay about it. It later became known under the title **“Civil Disobedience”** and influenced many people, including **Mahatma Gandhi** in India.

abschnitte.titel: Rosa Parks and the bus boycott
abschnitte.text: In **Montgomery**, the capital of **Alabama**, strict laws on **racial segregation** applied at that time. On 1 December 1955, **Rosa Parks** refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger. She was arrested. After that, many Black people boycotted the buses for more than a year. **Martin Luther King** became well known during this time. In 1963, in his **“Letter from Birmingham Jail”**, he defended non-violent breaking of unjust laws.

In a **sit-in**, people sit down and refuse to leave a place. The sit-ins of **1960** in **Greensboro** in the USA are famous. Black students sat down at lunch counters where only white people were served. They stayed in their seats even though they were not served. Soon people in many cities joined in.

In **1975**, opponents of nuclear power occupied the building site of the planned **Kaiseraugst nuclear power station** in the canton of **Aargau** for several weeks. Thousands of people took part without violence. In the end the power station was never built. Whether civil disobedience is justified in a democracy is still **judged differently** today. Supporters see it as a means against injustice, while opponents stress that laws must apply to everyone.

gewusst: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days.
In 1930, on the Salt March, Gandhi walked to the sea to protest against the British salt monopoly.

teile.einleitung: Popular sovereignty means that the highest power in the state comes from the people. This is a principle of every democracy. In Switzerland the people are especially strong, because they have the final say in votes.
wichtigste: In a democracy, power in the state comes from the people.
That is why in Switzerland the people are called the sovereign.
With 50,000 signatures in 100 days you can demand a referendum against a federal law.
A change to the Federal Constitution needs the approval of the people and the cantons.
A dictator usually takes power without the consent of the people.

abschnitte.text: In the past, kings said that their power came from God. Philosophers such as **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**, who was born in Geneva, put forward a different idea: power should come from the **people**. This is called **popular sovereignty**. Sovereign means “highest ruler”. This idea became especially important in the French Revolution.

In Switzerland people say that the people are the **sovereign**. The voters do not only elect parliament; they also decide on specific issues. There are **popular votes** several times a year. In them the people have the final say. This form is called **direct democracy**.

With a **referendum**, the people can bring a new federal law to a vote. This needs **50,000 signatures** in 100 days. With a **popular initiative** you can propose a change to the Federal Constitution; this needs 100,000 signatures. Every change to the Federal Constitution must be accepted by **the people and the cantons**. So nothing works without the people.

A **dictator** does not ask the people for permission before taking power. He takes it, often by force. Sometimes dictatorships do hold elections or votes, but without a real choice. Then they claim that the people are behind them. Real popular sovereignty needs free elections, freedom of expression and independent courts.

gewusst: Switzerland holds a very large number of national popular votes compared with the rest of the world.
In Switzerland the people have already voted on buying new fighter jets.

teile.einleitung: On 20 January 1942, senior officials and SS leaders met in a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin. They discussed how the murder of the Jews of Europe was to be organised. The minutes of this meeting are an important record of the Holocaust.
wichtigste: The Wannsee Conference took place in Berlin on 20 January 1942.
Reinhard Heydrich chaired the meeting, and Adolf Eichmann wrote the minutes.
Hermann Göring had given Heydrich the task of preparing it in July 1941.
The minutes listed around 11 million Jews throughout Europe.
The Jews in Switzerland were also listed, with the figure 18,000.
The mass murder had already begun; the meeting was about organisation.
Only the 16th of 30 copies of the minutes has survived.

abschnitte.text: The **Wannsee Conference** took place on **20 January 1942** in a villa on the Grosser Wannsee lake in Berlin. Around 15 men took part: state secretaries from ministries and leaders of the SS. The meeting had been called and was chaired by **Reinhard Heydrich**, head of the Reich Security Main Office. He wanted to establish his leading role in organising the mass murder. The meeting lasted only about an hour and a half.

On **31 July 1941**, **Hermann Göring** had given Heydrich the written task of preparing an “overall solution of the Jewish question”. Heydrich referred to this explicitly at the conference. In this way he wanted to show that he was in charge. The National Socialists used disguising words such as **“Final Solution”**. What they meant was the genocide of the Jews.

The conference is not regarded as the place where the genocide was **decided**. In the east, mass shootings and the first murders with gas had already begun. The conference was about **involving the ministries** and coordinating the **deportations**. That is why it shows how many parts of the state took part in the Holocaust.

**Adolf Eichmann** wrote the minutes. They listed around **11 million** Jews throughout Europe who were to be affected. Neutral countries such as **Switzerland**, with 18,000 Jews, were also listed, as well as Sweden and Spain. So the plans were aimed at all the Jews of Europe, not only those in the area under German control. Eichmann was convicted in Israel in 1962 and executed.

Of the 30 copies of the minutes, only the **16th** has survived. It was meant for **Martin Luther** of the Foreign Office. In March 1947 the US prosecutor **Robert Kempner** came across it in the files of the Foreign Office. At the time he was preparing the subsequent Nuremberg trials. The document became a key piece of evidence. Today the villa is a **memorial and education centre**.

gewusst: The official Martin Luther, whose copy survived, is not related to the reformer.
The memorial in the House of the Wannsee Conference was opened in 1992, 50 years after the meeting.

teile.einleitung: An arbitrary arrest means that someone is locked up without a legal reason or without a fair trial. Dictatorships often use such arrests against critics. That is why people have fought for centuries for laws that protect against arbitrary detention.
wichtigste: An arbitrary arrest is an arrest without a legal reason or court proceedings.
Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights forbids it.
The English Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 protected prisoners from arbitrary detention.
Before 1789 the French king had people locked up with lettres de cachet.
In Switzerland, the compulsory measures court decides on pre-trial detention.
Since 1991 a UN working group has investigated cases of arbitrary detention.

abschnitte.text: In an **arbitrary arrest**, someone is locked up without a legal reason or without a fair trial. Often the person is not even told what they are accused of. **Dictatorships** often do this to critics. **Incommunicado detention** is particularly dangerous: the prisoner has no contact with a lawyer or family. This increases the risk of torture and mistreatment.

Before the French Revolution, the French king could have people locked up without a trial. For this there were **lettres de cachet**, sealed orders from the king. With them, people were put, for example, into the **Bastille** in Paris without a court ruling. The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became a symbol against this arbitrary rule.

In England the **Habeas Corpus Act** was passed in **1679**. After that, a prisoner had to be brought before a **judge** quickly. The judge checked whether the detention was lawful. This principle influenced many later constitutions. Today **Article 9** of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights says: no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.

The **Federal Constitution** also protects against arbitrary detention. Anyone who is arrested must be told why and may have relatives informed. If the **public prosecutor's office** wants someone to remain in **pre-trial detention**, it has to apply for this. An independent **compulsory measures court** decides on it. In this way a court always checks whether the detention is necessary.

Since **1991** there has been the UN **Working Group on Arbitrary Detention**. It is part of the human rights system in **Geneva**. The working group examines complaints from all over the world. It can call on states to release prisoners. Closely related is **enforced disappearance**, in which people are secretly arrested and their whereabouts are concealed.

gewusst: “Habeas corpus” is Latin and means roughly “you shall have the body”, meaning: bring the prisoner before a court.
When the Bastille was stormed in 1789, only seven prisoners were still being held there.

teile.einleitung: From around 2017, many Uyghurs and other Muslims were held in camps in the Chinese region of Xinjiang. China speaks of education centres, but leaked documents and research show that the camps are based on force.
wichtigste: From 2016, party leader Chen Quanguo massively expanded the camp system.
The “China Cables” of 2019 contained internal instructions about the camps.
The “Xinjiang Police Files” of 2022 showed thousands of photos of detainees.
The researcher Adrian Zenz analysed Chinese documents.
In January 2021 the USA classified the actions as genocide.
Ilham Tohti was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2014.

abschnitte.text: **Chen Quanguo** became party leader of **Xinjiang** in 2016. Before that he had worked in **Tibet** and brought surveillance methods over from there. Under him, numerous **internment camps** were built. The German researcher **Adrian Zenz** analysed building tenders, job adverts for guards and statistics. In this way he made the scale of the camps visible. In 2021 China placed sanctions on him.

In 2019 an international network of journalists published the **“China Cables”**. They contained instructions on how camps were to be secured, escapes prevented and inmates re-educated. This contradicted the picture of voluntary schools. In 2022 the **“Xinjiang Police Files”** followed. This hacked police data contained thousands of **portrait photos** of prisoners, including young people and old people, as well as strict rules against escape.

The Uyghur economics professor **Ilham Tohti** had peacefully criticised the discrimination against the Uyghurs. In 2014 he was sentenced to **life imprisonment** for **“separatism”**. After that he received several international human rights prizes, including the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize.

On **19 January 2021**, US Secretary of State **Mike Pompeo** declared that China was committing **genocide** against the Uyghurs. The next administration confirmed this assessment. A US law of 2021 presumes in principle that goods from Xinjiang involve **forced labour**. Importers have to prove the opposite, otherwise the goods may not be brought into the country. China rejects all the accusations and speaks of measures against extremism.

gewusst: A large part of what is known about the camps comes from public Chinese documents.
Under the 2021 US law, the burden of proof is reversed: importers have to prove that no forced labour is involved.

teile.einleitung: The White Rose was a resistance group against the National Socialist dictatorship. It consisted mainly of students in Munich. With leaflets they called on people to stand up against Hitler, and they paid for it with their lives.
wichtigste: The White Rose was mainly active in Munich.
At its core were students, including Hans and Sophie Scholl.
Between 1942 and 1943 the group wrote six leaflets.
On 18 February 1943 Hans and Sophie Scholl were discovered in the university.
Sophie Scholl was executed at the age of 21.
Professor Kurt Huber helped to write the last leaflet.
The Allies dropped millions of copies of the last leaflet over Germany.

abschnitte.text: The **White Rose** was formed in **Munich**. At its core were young **students** at the university. **Hans Scholl**, who was studying medicine, founded the group with **Alexander Schmorell**. Others who joined included Christoph Probst and Willi Graf. Hans's younger sister **Sophie Scholl** studied **biology and philosophy** in Munich from 1942 and joined the group.

The group resisted with **leaflets**. It secretly wrote, copied and distributed them. Between 1942 and 1943, **six** leaflets were produced. They were distributed in several cities or sent by post. The texts called on people to think about the crimes of the regime and to resist.

The group was supported by **Kurt Huber**. He was a professor of philosophy and musicology at the University of Munich. Huber helped to write the **sixth leaflet**. He was later arrested too. In 1943 he was also executed.

On **18 February 1943**, Hans and Sophie Scholl laid out leaflets in the university. They threw a pile into the **atrium**. A caretaker saw them and reported them. The two were arrested and, together with Christoph Probst, sentenced to death. On **22 February 1943** they were executed. Sophie Scholl was **21 years** old.

The last leaflet reached **England** via Scandinavia. In 1943 British aircraft dropped millions of copies of it over Germany. It was titled **“Manifesto of the Munich Students”**. In this way many people learned about the White Rose. Today in Munich, for example, the **Geschwister-Scholl-Platz** and many schools remember the group.

gewusst: In Germany, a great many schools are named after Sophie and Hans Scholl.
In front of the University of Munich, White Rose leaflets are set into the ground as a memorial.

teile.einleitung: An electoral autocracy is a state in which elections do take place, but they are not really free and fair. Those in power let people vote but make sure that they keep power. Experts have described many techniques by which this is done.
wichtigste: In an electoral autocracy there are elections but no fair competition.
The political scientist Andreas Schedler described a “menu of manipulation”.
In the GDR, people approved the single list by “Zettelfalten” (folding the slip).
In the GDR local elections in May 1989, civil rights activists proved electoral fraud.
In North Korea there is only one candidate per constituency.
Gerrymandering means drawing constituency boundaries to your own advantage.
In 2022 the European Parliament described Hungary as a “hybrid regime of electoral autocracy”.

abschnitte.text: An **autocracy** is a state in which a few people hold power. In an **electoral autocracy**, elections still take place. But they are not free and fair. The political scientist **Andreas Schedler** coined the term electoral authoritarianism. In 2002 he described a **“menu of manipulation”**: techniques that rulers use to control elections without abolishing them.

In the GDR there was only a **single list** of the National Front. You approved it by simply folding the ballot paper and putting it in the box. This was called **“Zettelfalten”** (folding the slip). Anyone who used the voting booth stood out and made themselves look suspicious. In the **local elections of 7 May 1989**, the leadership announced almost 99 per cent approval. Civil rights activists had observed the counting and counted many more votes against.

After the German army marched in, Austria voted in **April 1938** on “Anschluss” (union) with Germany. The official result was around **99.7 per cent** Yes, under massive propaganda and without a truly secret ballot. In **North Korea**, in elections to the Supreme People's Assembly, there is only **one candidate** per constituency. Voters can only approve. The official approval rates are close to 100 per cent.

Elections are not always openly rigged. Some governments draw **constituency boundaries** to their own advantage. This is called **gerrymandering**. The name goes back to **Elbridge Gerry**, who as Governor of Massachusetts in 1812 signed a plan with a district shaped like a salamander. Other methods are controlling the media or excluding candidates.

In **September 2022** the **European Parliament** adopted a report on **Hungary**. In it, it described the country as a “hybrid regime of electoral autocracy”. Among other things, the report criticised the concentration of media ownership and restrictions on the judiciary. The Hungarian government rejected this assessment. Election observers such as the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights check whether elections are free and fair.

gewusst: Gerrymandering is a made-up word from the name Gerry and the word salamander.
The OSCE's office for election observation is based in Warsaw.

teile.einleitung: Surveillance means that someone watches people, listens in on them or collects their data. Dictatorships often watch their citizens very closely to find critics. In democracies, data protection protects people from this.
wichtigste: In a surveillance state, the government watches what people do and say.
A bug is a small hidden microphone for listening in.
The Stasi in the GDR tapped telephones and secretly opened letters.
In the novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four”, Big Brother watches everyone.
People who feel watched often stop saying what they think.
In Switzerland, the Secret Files Scandal came to light in 1989.
Data protection protects personal information from being accessed by others.

abschnitte.text: In a **surveillance state**, the government watches what people do and say. There is hardly any **privacy**. In this way dictatorships want to find out who is against them. Anyone who knows they are constantly being watched becomes careful. Many people then no longer dare to say what they **think** openly.

When **tapping**, conversations are secretly listened in on. For this, secret services hid **bugs** in flats, meaning tiny microphones. The **Stasi** in the GDR tapped many telephones. Every day it also opened many **letters** and parcels. Afterwards it stuck them shut again so that nobody would notice.

The English writer **George Orwell** wrote the novel **“Nineteen Eighty-Four”**. In it, pictures of **Big Brother** hang everywhere. Beneath them it says that he is watching you. The state in this book controls everything, even thoughts. The novel is regarded as a famous warning against the surveillance state.

Today there are new technologies. Cameras with **facial recognition** can automatically identify people in a crowd. Some states use this to find opponents. Mobile phones and the internet also leave many data traces. That is why it matters who is allowed to collect and use this data.

abschnitte.titel: Secret files and data protection in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: There was a surveillance scandal in Switzerland too. In **1989** it came out that for decades the federal police had kept index cards, so-called **Fichen**, on a very large number of people. This is called the **Secret Files Scandal** (Fichenaffäre). After that the rules became stricter. Today a special law governs **data protection**. It makes sure that nobody collects personal data without permission.

gewusst: The Stasi even collected smell samples from some people in jars so that dogs could recognise them later.
The term “Big Brother” from the novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four” later became the name of a television programme.

teile.einleitung: Saddam Hussein was President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. He ruled as a dictator with violence and a large secret service, fought several wars and was overthrown in 2003 by an invasion led by the USA.
wichtigste: Saddam Hussein belonged to the Baath Party.
In 1979 he officially became President of Iraq.
From 1980 to 1988 he waged war against Iran.
In 1988 he had the Kurdish town of Halabja attacked with poison gas.
In 1990 he had Kuwait occupied.
He was overthrown in 2003 and executed in 2006.

abschnitte.text: **Saddam Hussein** came from the area around **Tikrit**. He belonged to the **Baath Party**, which came to power through a coup in 1968. Even then Saddam was the strongman behind the president. In **July 1979** he took over the **presidency** himself. He built up a large **personality cult** and a feared secret service.

In **1980** Iraq attacked its neighbour **Iran**. This **First Gulf War** lasted eight years until **1988**. Hundreds of thousands of people died without either side winning. Towards the end of the war, Saddam had the **Kurdish** town of **Halabja** attacked with **poison gas**. Around 5000 people died.

In **August 1990** the Iraqi army marched into the small, oil-rich neighbouring country of **Kuwait**. The UN demanded a withdrawal. An international coalition led by the **USA** drove out the Iraqi troops at the beginning of 1991. After that, strict **sanctions** applied against Iraq for many years.

In **March 2003** the USA and its allies attacked Iraq. Their main justification was weapons of mass destruction, but these were never found. The war was therefore highly **controversial** internationally. In April **Baghdad** fell. The toppling of a large statue of Saddam in **Firdos Square** became the symbol of the end of his rule.

In **December 2003**, US soldiers found Saddam in a camouflaged **hole in the ground** on a farm near Tikrit. A special Iraqi court sentenced him to death for the killing of 148 people in the town of **Dujail**. On **30 December 2006** he was executed. After that, Iraq remained marked by violence for a long time.

gewusst: In a referendum in 2002, Saddam supposedly had himself confirmed with 100 per cent of the vote.
Saddam had parts of the ancient city of Babylon rebuilt and his name stamped into the bricks.

teile.einleitung: Election observers check independently whether an election is free and fair. They watch closely in the polling station and then write a report. The OSCE, which Switzerland also belongs to, plays a particularly important role in this.
wichtigste: Election observers check whether an election is free, fair and follows the rules.
The OSCE often sends observers to countries in Europe and Central Asia.
The OSCE's ODIHR is based in Warsaw.
Long-term observers are in the country weeks before the election.
Ballot stuffing is an example of electoral fraud.
Some authoritarian states do not invite independent observers.

abschnitte.text: **Election observers** check independently whether an election is **free and fair**. They do not interfere but watch closely. Afterwards they write a **report** with praise, criticism and recommendations. This helps countries improve their elections. At the same time, the world finds out whether a result is credible.

The **Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe** (OSCE) observes many elections in its member countries. These include states in Europe, North America and Central Asia. **Switzerland** is also a member and sends experts on such missions. The observation is organised mainly by the **Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights** (ODIHR). It is based in **Warsaw**, Poland.

**Long-term observers** arrive in the country weeks before the election. They follow the election campaign, the media reports and the preparations for the election. **Short-term observers** only travel there for election day. They visit many polling stations. In this way an overall picture of the whole election is built up.

In the polling station, the observers check whether every person can vote in **secret**. They also check whether the votes are **counted correctly**. One sign of fraud is when someone puts several ballot papers into the ballot box. This is called **ballot stuffing**. They write down observations like this carefully.

abschnitte.titel: When nobody is allowed to watch
abschnitte.text: Some **authoritarian states** do not invite independent observers. Without observers, fraud is easier to hide. The government can then claim a good result. If the result is fixed in advance because there is no real choice, it is called a **sham election**. Election observers clearly criticise such elections.

gewusst: Elections in Switzerland have also been assessed by OSCE experts.
Election observers may not interfere or tell anyone whom to vote for.

teile.einleitung: Turkmenistan is a country in Central Asia on the Caspian Sea. It is ruled in an authoritarian way and is known for an extreme personality cult around its presidents.
wichtigste: The capital is called Ashgabat and is known for its white marble buildings.
The first president, Saparmurat Niyazov, called himself “Turkmenbashi”.
Niyazov named months after himself and his mother.
His book “Ruhnama” was compulsory reading in schools.
In 2022 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow handed over the office to his son Serdar.
Turkmenistan has huge reserves of natural gas.

abschnitte.text: Turkmenistan is in **Central Asia** and was part of the Soviet Union until 1991. A large part of the country is covered by the **Karakum** desert, which means “black sand”. The capital **Ashgabat** is known for its many buildings made of **white marble**. Many showy buildings are meant to display the government's power.

The first president, **Saparmurat Niyazov**, gave himself the title **Turkmenbashi**, “leader of the Turkmens”. He had himself worshipped like a ruler. He even named **months** after himself and after his mother. His book **“Ruhnama”**, the “Book of the Soul”, was compulsory reading in schools and even for the driving test. Niyazov ruled until his death in 2006.

Niyazov was followed by **Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow**. A strong **personality cult** grew up around him too. In 2022 he handed over the presidency to his son **Serdar Berdimuhamedow**. So power stayed in the family. There are no free elections, no real opposition and no independent media.

abschnitte.titel: Natural gas and the Gates of Hell
abschnitte.text: Turkmenistan has some of the **largest natural gas reserves** in the world. The government uses the money to pay for magnificent buildings. In the Karakum lies the burning gas crater near **Darvaza**. It has been burning for decades because natural gas escapes there, and it is called the **“Gates of Hell”**. It is a well-known sight.

gewusst: Under Niyazov, one month bore his mother's name.
The Darvaza gas crater has been burning non-stop for decades.

teile.einleitung: In electoral fraud, election results are deliberately falsified. Anyone who does this cheats the voters and steals their vote. Dictators often use electoral fraud to pretend that the people elected them.
wichtigste: In electoral fraud, election results are deliberately falsified.
Typical methods are wrongly counted votes, stuffed ballot boxes or forged electoral rolls.
Putting pressure on voters and buying votes are also part of electoral fraud.
Dictatorships often hold sham elections in which the result has been decided beforehand.
International observers, for example from the OSCE, monitor elections in many countries.
In Switzerland electoral fraud is a criminal offence.
Secret ballots and public counting protect against fraud.

abschnitte.text: In **electoral fraud**, the result of an election or vote is deliberately changed. This can happen when votes are cast, counted or reported. The aim is usually for a particular person or party to win. This violates the most important principle of **democracy**: the people decide.

Sometimes ballot boxes are filled with ballot papers beforehand; this is called **ballot stuffing**. Other tricks are votes cast in the names of dead people, people who vote several times, or ballot papers that simply disappear. Voters are also intimidated or bribed with money. When the votes are counted, the figures can simply be reported wrongly at the end.

Many dictators hold elections so that they look good to the world. But often only one party is allowed, or rival candidates are arrested beforehand. Results of over 90 per cent are then a typical warning sign of a **sham election**. After the 2020 presidential election in Belarus, hundreds of thousands took to the streets because they thought the official result was rigged.

Important safeguards are the **secret ballot**, independent electoral authorities and public counting. Representatives of different parties watch the counting. The OSCE sends **election observers** to many countries to check that everything is done correctly. Journalists and statisticians can also spot suspicious results.

In Switzerland most people vote by post, and the envelope is checked with a voting card. Volunteers in the **polling office** count the votes in the municipalities. Electoral fraud is forbidden in the Swiss Criminal Code and can be punished with prison. If results are very close, a **recount** is sometimes ordered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sealed container into which the ballot papers are put.
Nobody may know whom a person voted for.
Neutral experts who check whether an election is fair.
An election whose result has been decided beforehand.

gewusst: Statisticians can sometimes detect fraud because certain final digits appear suspiciously often in the results.
In some countries, a voter's finger is marked with ink that does not come off for days, so that nobody can vote twice.
In Switzerland there are elections and votes on several voting Sundays every year, and cases of fraud are very rare.

teile.einleitung: The Securitate was the secret police of the communist dictatorship in Romania. It watched the population, persecuted people who thought differently and, especially under Nicolae Ceaușescu, was regarded as one of the harshest secret services in the Eastern Bloc.
wichtigste: The Securitate was the state security service of the Socialist Republic of Romania.
It was founded in August 1948 with Soviet help.
From 1983 all typewriters had to be registered with the police.
The writer Herta Müller was spied on for years.
General Ion Mihai Pacepa defected to the USA in 1978.
Protests in support of the pastor László Tőkés set off the revolution in 1989.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, the communists came to power in Romania. In August 1948 the **Securitate** was founded with the help of the Soviet Union. It was meant to secure communist rule. To do this it monitored letters, telephones and conversations and used a large network of **informers**. Anyone who was considered an opponent could be arrested.

Especially in the early years, many people were held in prisons and labour camps. In the prison of **Pitești**, from 1949 to 1951, students in particular were forced to give up their beliefs and to mistreat fellow prisoners. This so-called **Pitești experiment** is regarded as one of the cruellest re-education programmes in the Eastern Bloc.

Under **Nicolae Ceaușescu**, control became tighter and tighter. From 1983 every **typewriter** had to be registered, and a sample of its type had to be handed in. In this way the Securitate could trace critical leaflets back to a particular machine. In 1978 the high-ranking general **Ion Mihai Pacepa** defected to the USA. He was deputy head of the foreign intelligence service and later described the inner workings of the dictatorship in the book “Red Horizons”.

The writer **Herta Müller** comes from the German-speaking minority in the **Banat**. She refused to work with the Securitate and was therefore spied on and harassed for years. Later she left Romania and lived in Germany. In her books she wrote about the persecution. In 2009 she received the **Nobel Prize in Literature**.

In December 1989, the Hungarian Reformed pastor **László Tőkés** was to be evicted from his flat in **Timișoara**. Members of his church and other citizens formed a human chain to protect him. This turned into a popular uprising that spread across the whole country. Ceaușescu was overthrown, and the Securitate was dissolved afterwards.

gewusst: The registration of typewriters is a well-known example of how far surveillance went in Romania.
Ion Mihai Pacepa is regarded as one of the highest-ranking defectors from the Eastern Bloc.

teile.einleitung: Ruhollah Khomeini was a Shiite cleric from Iran. In 1979 he led the Islamic Revolution, which overthrew the Shah, and until his death in 1989 he was the Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
wichtigste: Khomeini held the rank of Grand Ayatollah.
Because of his criticism of the Shah's White Revolution, he had to go into exile in 1964.
From 1965 to 1978 he lived in Najaf in Iraq, and then in France.
On 1 February 1979 he returned to Tehran.
In 1989 he issued a fatwa against Salman Rushdie.
After his death in 1989, Ali Khamenei became Supreme Leader.

abschnitte.text: **Ruhollah Khomeini** was born in 1902. In Shiite Islam he reached the rank of **Grand Ayatollah**. The title ayatollah means “sign of God”. A grand ayatollah is regarded as the highest religious authority, whom the faithful follow. Khomeini criticised the **Shah**, the King of Iran, and his close ties with the USA.

In 1963 the Shah launched the **White Revolution**, with a land reform and votes for women. Khomeini strongly rejected it and was sent into **exile** in **1964**. From 1965 he lived in **Najaf** in Iraq, a centre of Shiite learning. There he developed his teaching that a religious legal scholar should lead the state. In 1978 he moved to **France**, near Paris.

His sermons were recorded on **cassette tapes** and secretly copied in Iran. In this way they reached millions despite censorship. In 1978 there were huge protests against the Shah, who left the country at the beginning of 1979. On **1 February 1979**, Khomeini returned in triumph to **Tehran**. Soon afterwards the **Islamic Republic** was proclaimed.

Khomeini became **Supreme Leader** and had the final say in the state. Opponents were persecuted, and many were executed. In the summer of **1988**, thousands of political prisoners were executed in the prisons after short interrogations. This is regarded as one of the worst crimes of the Islamic Republic. Many Iranians still revere Khomeini today; others see him as a dictator.

In 1989 Khomeini issued a **fatwa**, a religious ruling, against the writer **Salman Rushdie**. The reason was his novel “The Satanic Verses”. Rushdie had to live under police protection for years. Khomeini died in June 1989. The Assembly of Experts chose **Ali Khamenei** as his successor.

gewusst: In exile in France, Khomeini gave so many interviews that he became known all over the world.
Millions of people came to his funeral in Tehran.

teile.einleitung: The Tiananmen Square massacre was the violent crushing of a large protest movement in Beijing in 1989. For weeks, students and workers had demonstrated for more freedom in Tiananmen Square. During the night of 3 to 4 June 1989, the military crushed the protests with tanks and weapons.
wichtigste: In 1989, protests for more freedom in Tiananmen Square in Beijing were crushed by the military.
The protests began in April 1989 after the death of the popular politician Hu Yaobang.
Students in particular demanded freedom of expression, freedom of the press and less corruption.
On 20 May 1989 the government declared martial law.
During the night of 3 to 4 June, soldiers with tanks advanced into the city centre.
How many people died is still unclear today; estimates range from hundreds to several thousand.
In China the event is still hardly talked about and is strictly censored.

abschnitte.text: **Tiananmen Square**, meaning “Square of the Gate of Heavenly Peace”, is in the centre of **Beijing**, the capital of China. It is one of the largest squares in the world. In the spring of 1989, tens of thousands of people, at times even hundreds of thousands, gathered there for weeks. There were similar protests in many other cities in China too.

The trigger was the death on 15 April 1989 of the politician **Hu Yaobang**, who was regarded as a reformer. Students mourned him and soon demanded more **democracy** and freedom of expression and of the press. Many people were also angry about corruption and rising prices. Later, workers joined in, and some students went on hunger strike.

The leadership of the **Communist Party** saw its power threatened and declared **martial law** on 20 May. During the night of 3 to 4 June 1989, soldiers and tanks advanced onto the square and the surrounding streets. They shot at demonstrators and onlookers. The exact number of deaths is unknown; estimates range from several hundred to several thousand.

On 5 June 1989, an unknown man with shopping bags stood alone in front of a column of tanks. Photos and film footage of this **“Tank Man”** went around the world. To this day nobody knows for certain who he was and what happened to him. The picture became a symbol of brave, non-violent resistance.

After the crackdown, many participants were arrested, and some fled abroad. In China the subject is still heavily **censored** today, and search terms about it are blocked on the internet. Many young people in China hardly know about the events. In Hong Kong, tens of thousands remembered the victims with candles every year until these commemorations were banned from 2020.

begriffe.erklaerung: Emergency rules under which the military gets a lot of power and rights are restricted.
When people voluntarily stop eating as a protest.
When the state controls and forbids what may be published.
A gathering of many people who show their opinion together.

gewusst: On the square, the students built a statue about ten metres high, the “Goddess of Democracy”, which was destroyed by the soldiers.
In the middle of the protests, the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev visited Beijing, which is why many foreign journalists were there.

teile.einleitung: A whistleblower is a person who makes wrongdoing or abuse of power public. Usually they work in a company or an authority and discover something illegal or dangerous there. The word comes from English and literally means “someone who blows the whistle”.
wichtigste: A whistleblower makes wrongdoing or abuse of power public.
They are often employees who discover wrongdoing in their company or authority.
Whistleblowers often risk their job, lawsuits or even prison.
Well-known whistleblowers are Daniel Ellsberg, Edward Snowden and Chelsea Manning.
Whistleblowing is especially dangerous in dictatorships.
In 2019 the European Union adopted a directive to protect whistleblowers.
So far Switzerland has no specific law that fully protects whistleblowers.

abschnitte.text: The English word **whistleblower** means something like someone who blows a whistle, like a referee who blows for a foul. In German they are also called **“Hinweisgeber”** (informants). It means someone who passes on information about fraud, corruption, dangers or crimes. Often the person first reports the wrongdoing internally and only later turns to the authorities or the media.

In 1971 the military expert **Daniel Ellsberg** passed secret papers about the Vietnam War to newspapers: the Pentagon Papers. In 2013 **Edward Snowden** revealed that the US intelligence agency, the NSA, was collecting telephone and internet data around the world. He has lived in Russia since then, because he faces a trial in the USA. Chelsea Manning passed secret military documents to the Wikileaks platform and was convicted for it.

In 1997 the security guard Christoph Meili at the UBS bank in Zurich rescued files from being shredded that had to do with accounts of Holocaust victims. He lost his job and later moved to the USA. In 2007 two employees of the City of Zurich's social services department made wrongdoing public and were at first convicted of **breach of official secrecy**. Cases like these show how difficult the situation of whistleblowers can be.

Whistleblowers are often caught between two duties: they are supposed to keep their employer's secrets, but they want to prevent wrongdoing. Many lose their job or are shut out by colleagues. Since 2019 the EU has required its member states to protect whistleblowers from **dismissal** and discrimination. In Switzerland, parliament rejected a proposed law on this in 2020, but many companies and authorities have set up their own **reporting offices**.

In a dictatorship, whistleblowers are in great danger because there are no free courts and no free press. Anyone who uncovers abuse of power is quickly persecuted as a traitor. Even so, information about prisons, torture or corruption keeps reaching other countries. Brave people like these help the world to understand what is happening in closed-off states.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a whistleblower; in German “Hinweisgeber”.
The duty of state employees not to pass on confidential information.
An office where you can report wrongdoing confidentially.
When someone abuses their power to gain advantages, for example through bribery.

gewusst: The story of Daniel Ellsberg and the Pentagon Papers has been made into films several times.
Many large companies in Switzerland now offer anonymous reporting platforms on the internet.
The word whistleblower recalls police officers who used to draw attention to crimes with a whistle.

teile.einleitung: Salvador Allende was a doctor and politician in Chile. In 1970 he became the first avowed Marxist to be elected president in free elections. His government ended with a military coup on 11 September 1973.
wichtigste: Allende was a doctor by profession.
He won the 1970 presidential election with around 36 per cent of the vote.
His alliance of parties was called Unidad Popular.
In 1971 his government had the copper mines nationalised.
Every child was to receive half a litre of milk a day.
Allende died during the coup in the La Moneda presidential palace.

abschnitte.text: **Salvador Allende** was born in 1908. He studied medicine and worked as a **doctor**. In doing so he saw how poor many people in Chile were. He became one of the best-known politicians of the **Socialist Party**. He stood unsuccessfully for president three times before winning in 1970.

In September 1970 Allende won the election with around **36 per cent** of the vote. Because he did not have an absolute majority, **parliament** had to confirm him. What was special was that an avowed **Marxist** became president in a free election. At that time this was almost unique in the world. His alliance of left-wing parties was called **Unidad Popular**, Popular Unity.

Allende wanted to turn Chile into a **socialist** country by democratic means. The large **copper mines** belonged mainly to US companies. In 1971 parliament voted unanimously to **nationalise** them. A well-known programme promised every child **half a litre of milk** a day to fight malnutrition. Land was also redistributed.

Soon Chile fell into a severe **economic crisis**, with high inflation and empty shelves. There were big strikes, and society was deeply divided. The **USA** rejected Allende's government and supported his opponents. To this day, Allende's policies are judged in very different ways.

On **11 September 1973** the military staged a coup. Allende stayed in the presidential palace **La Moneda** in Santiago and gave a last radio address. When soldiers stormed the building, he died. Investigations later showed that he took his own life. After that, a military dictatorship under Augusto Pinochet ruled until 1990.

gewusst: The poet Pablo Neruda, a supporter of Allende, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
Today there is a monument to Allende in front of the La Moneda presidential palace.

teile.einleitung: Robert Mugabe led Zimbabwe in southern Africa from 1980 to 2017. At first he was seen as a hero of liberation from white minority rule; later he ruled in an increasingly authoritarian way and led the country into a severe economic crisis.
wichtigste: As a British colony, Zimbabwe was called Southern Rhodesia, and later Rhodesia.
In 1980 Zimbabwe became independent, and Mugabe became prime minister.
From 1987 to 2017 he was president; his party was called ZANU-PF.
From 2000 many farms belonging to white owners were taken away from them.
In 2008 inflation reached an extreme peak.
In 2017 the army forced him to resign, and Emmerson Mnangagwa succeeded him.

abschnitte.text: As a British colony, the country was called **Southern Rhodesia**, later just **Rhodesia**. In 1965 the white minority government under **Ian Smith** declared independence unilaterally, and the Black majority had hardly any rights. At that time Mugabe was imprisoned for more than ten years. After a long **war of liberation**, the country became independent as **Zimbabwe** in **1980**.

Mugabe won the first elections in 1980 and became **Prime Minister**, and from 1987 he was **President**. His party **ZANU-PF** grew out of the liberation movement ZANU and has governed since independence. Over time, Mugabe hardly tolerated any disagreement. In the 1980s, troops in the Matabeleland region acted brutally against suspected opponents, and thousands died. Elections were accompanied by violence and accusations of fraud.

A large part of the fertile land belonged to white large landowners. From the year **2000**, the government had many of these **farms** occupied and taken away, often by force. Many new owners had no experience or equipment. After that, **agriculture** collapsed badly, and the country could no longer feed itself.

The economic crisis led to extreme **inflation**: money lost its value faster and faster. In 2008 there were banknotes of **100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars**, and still you could buy little with them. In 2009 the country's own currency was given up, and people paid with foreign money such as the US dollar.

In **November 2017** the **military** took control. Mugabe then resigned at the age of 93. His long-time vice-president **Emmerson Mnangagwa** became president. Mugabe died in **September 2019** at the age of 95 in **Singapore**, where he often had medical treatment.

gewusst: Mugabe was originally a teacher and gained several university degrees, some of them while he was in prison.
Zimbabwe is named after the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, an ancient stone city.

teile.einleitung: The social credit system is a project of the Chinese government to rate the behaviour of citizens, companies and authorities. It is not a single points system but a patchwork of many lists and sub-systems.
wichtigste: In 2014 China's State Council presented a plan up to 2020.
The official aim is more “trustworthiness” in society and the economy.
Anyone who does not comply with court rulings can be put on a blacklist.
Those affected may then not buy plane or high-speed train tickets, for example.
A large part of the system rates companies.
Every company has an 18-digit social credit code.

abschnitte.text: In 2014 the **Chinese State Council** presented a draft plan for the years 2014 to 2020. In it, it announced that the **trustworthiness** of citizens, companies and authorities would be rated. Officially, the system is meant to fight **fraud**, **breach of contract** and **counterfeiting**. Critics also see it as a means of steering people's behaviour and punishing those who step out of line.

Anyone who does not comply with a court ruling, for example by not paying debts, can be put on a **blacklist** as a **dishonest debtor**. Those affected may then not book flights or high-speed trains, among other things. Such lists exist for different areas. They are an important part of what is called social credit.

Many cities have started their own trials. The coastal city of **Rongcheng** in **Shandong** province became well known. There all adults were given a starting balance of **1000 points**. Good behaviour earns extra points, and offences cost points. Experts stress that there is no single score for all 1.4 billion people.

A large part of the system concerns **companies**. Since 2015, every company and organisation has had an **18-digit social credit code**. Offences are also stored under this number, for example concerning taxes, environmental rules or product safety. Bad ratings can lead to more inspections or to exclusion from contracts.

**Sesame Credit**, also called Zhima Credit, was introduced in 2015 by **Ant Financial**, a subsidiary of the online company Alibaba. It rates customers' **creditworthiness**, similar to credit checks in other countries. It is a company service and not part of the state system. In reports, however, the two are often mixed up.

gewusst: The well-known image of a single score for every person in China is not accurate.
In Rongcheng every adult started with 1000 points.

teile.einleitung: Totalitarianism is a particularly extreme form of dictatorship in which the state controls almost every area of people's lives. Not only politics but also school, work, free time, art and even thoughts are meant to be steered. Well-known examples are National Socialist Germany and the Soviet Union under Stalin.
wichtigste: Totalitarian regimes control almost all areas of life; authoritarian ones usually only politics.
The word comes from the Latin “totus”, which means “whole”.
A single party, a state ideology, a secret police and propaganda are typical.
Children and young people are also brought up in state organisations.
Well-known examples are the Nazi regime, the Soviet Union under Stalin and North Korea.
The philosopher Hannah Arendt studied totalitarianism in a famous book in 1951.
George Orwell described an invented totalitarian state in his novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four”.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **“totus”**, which means “whole”. A **totalitarian state** wants to take hold of and shape the whole person. It dictates what people should think, read, believe and celebrate. There is hardly any private life in which the state does not interfere.

There are different kinds of dictatorship. An **authoritarian dictatorship** mainly controls politics: elections and criticism are forbidden, but in everyday life it often leaves people some freedom. A **totalitarian regime**, on the other hand, controls almost every area of life, from work to school to free time. It does not just want to rule people but to turn them into convinced supporters.

Totalitarian states usually have a single permitted party with a powerful leader at the top. There is an **ideology** that is supposed to explain everything and that everyone has to believe in. A secret police watches people, and the media are full of **propaganda**. Children are brought up from an early age in youth organisations such as the Hitler Youth or the Soviet Pioneers.

The word appeared in the 1920s in **Italy**, where Benito Mussolini spoke of a “totalitarian state”. The main examples are considered to be Germany under **Adolf Hitler** from 1933 to 1945 and the Soviet Union under **Joseph Stalin**. North Korea and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge are also often described as totalitarian. In these states, millions of people were persecuted, imprisoned or killed.

In 1951 the German-American philosopher **Hannah Arendt** published a famous book on the origins of totalitarianism. In it she studied how National Socialism and Stalinism could come about. In 1949 the British writer **George Orwell** showed in the novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four” how a state that watches everything destroys people's lives. Both works are still read in schools and universities today.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the state wants to control all areas of life.
When a government holds power alone but does not control every area of life.
A fixed world view that is supposed to explain everything.
A word for a government, often an undemocratic one.

gewusst: As a Jew, Hannah Arendt herself had to flee from the National Socialists and later lived in the USA.
Terms from Orwell's novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four”, such as “Big Brother”, are often used today when talking about surveillance.

teile.einleitung: A surveillance state watches its citizens comprehensively and in secret. The best-known example in Europe is the GDR with its secret service, the Stasi. But in Switzerland too, a surveillance scandal caused outrage in 1989.
wichtigste: The Stasi headquarters were in Berlin-Lichtenberg.
Its motto was “Shield and sword of the party”.
In the autumn of 1989 the Stasi had around 91,000 full-time staff.
Erich Mielke ran the Stasi from 1957 to 1989.
In the Secret Files Scandal of 1989 it became known that around 900,000 files had been created.
On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the “snooping state”.
Since 1992 the people affected have been allowed to read their Stasi files.

abschnitte.text: The GDR's **Ministry for State Security**, **Stasi** for short, was both a secret service and a secret police force. Its headquarters were on Normannenstrasse in **Berlin-Lichtenberg**, where there is a museum today. Its motto was **“Shield and sword of the party”**. So the Stasi served the SED party and not the citizens. From **1957 to 1989**, **Erich Mielke** ran the ministry.

In the autumn of 1989, around **91,000** people worked full-time for the Stasi. On top of that there were many **unofficial collaborators**. These were citizens who secretly reported on neighbours, colleagues or even friends. In this way files were created on a great many people. Since **1992** the people affected have been allowed to read their files. Since 2021 the records have been part of the German **Federal Archives**.

abschnitte.titel: The Secret Files Scandal in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In **1989** a parliamentary commission of inquiry revealed that since 1900 the authorities had created around **900,000 Fichen**. Fichen are index cards with information about people and organisations. Those recorded were often left-wingers, trade unionists and foreigners. On **3 March 1990**, around 30,000 people protested in Federal Square in **Bern** against the “snooping state”. Many demanded to see their own file.

As early as around **1791**, the English philosopher **Jeremy Bentham** designed a special prison, the **Panopticon**. From a tower in the middle, a guard can watch all the prisoners without them seeing him. Because they never know whether they are being watched at that moment, they always behave as expected. This idea is often used to explain the effect of surveillance. In “Nineteen Eighty-Four” from 1949, George Orwell also described a state in which **Big Brother** watches everyone.

Modern surveillance states use new technology. Cameras with **facial recognition** compare faces with databases. **China** uses this technology especially often. The internet and mobile phones also provide a lot of data. In democracies there is therefore debate about how much surveillance is needed for security and how **privacy** can be protected.

gewusst: The Stasi left behind so many files that they would be more than 100 kilometres long if placed in a row.
After the Secret Files Scandal, tens of thousands of people in Switzerland were able to ask to see their own file.

teile.einleitung: After the end of apartheid, South Africa wanted to deal with the crimes of the past. For this, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up under Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Its main aim was not to punish but to bring the truth to light and to reconcile society.
wichtigste: The commission was based on a law from 1995.
From 1996 it was led by Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
It investigated human rights violations from 1960 to 1994.
It consisted of three committees: human rights violations, amnesty and reparation.
Around 7000 applications for amnesty were received, and only a small part was granted.
In 1998 the commission presented its final report.

abschnitte.text: Under **apartheid**, people in South Africa were separated and disadvantaged according to the colour of their skin. In 1994 **Nelson Mandela** became the country's first Black president. Many people now wanted to know what had happened during the years of oppression. In 1995 parliament passed the **Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act**. It formed the basis for the commission.

From 1996 the commission was led by the Anglican Archbishop **Desmond Tutu**. He had received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984. Tutu shaped the commission's focus on **reconciliation**. The period investigated ran from **March 1960** to **May 1994**. It began with the month of the **Sharpeville massacre** and ended with Mandela taking office.

The commission consisted of **three committees**. One heard the victims of **human rights violations**. A second decided on **amnesty**, meaning freedom from punishment for perpetrators. A third proposed **reparation** and rehabilitation for the victims. Many hearings were public and were broadcast on radio and television.

Perpetrators could apply for **amnesty** if they fully disclosed their deeds and these had political motives. Around **7000 applications** were received. Only a small part, about 850, were granted. Many applications did not meet the conditions. This approach was controversial: some victims would rather have seen punishments, while others valued finally learning the truth.

The work was based above all on the idea of **restorative justice**. The focus was on healing victims and society, not on punishment. The African term **Ubuntu**, which means humanity and community, was often mentioned in this context. In **1998** the commission presented its final report. It became a model for many other countries.

gewusst: At some hearings Desmond Tutu himself wept when victims told of their suffering.
The commission heard not only victims of the government but also victims of acts by the liberation movements.

teile.einleitung: The Stasi Records Archive holds the files of the GDR's state security service. People can read there what the secret police collected about them.
wichtigste: The files come from the Ministry for State Security, Stasi for short.
The first Federal Commissioner for the records was Joachim Gauck.
Since January 1992, the people affected have been able to look at their files.
Placed in a row, the files would be around 111 kilometres long.
Torn-up files lie in around 15,000 sacks.
Since June 2021 the archive has been part of the Federal Archives.

abschnitte.text: For decades the GDR's **Ministry for State Security**, **Stasi** for short, watched the population. It collected huge amounts of files, index cards, photos and sound recordings. The documents alone would stretch about **111 kilometres** if placed in a row. An important part comes from **unofficial collaborators (IM)**. They secretly spied on friends, colleagues and even family members.

During the **Wende**, the period of change in 1989 and 1990, the Stasi tried to destroy files. Civil rights activists wanted to stop this. In January 1990 they occupied the Stasi headquarters on **Normannenstrasse** in **Berlin-Lichtenberg**. A large part of the archive is there today. Many files were torn up by hand. These scraps lie in around **15,000 sacks** and are being pieced together by hand and with computers.

The **Stasi Records Act** came into force at the end of December 1991. Since **2 January 1992**, the people affected have been able to apply to see their files. In this way many found out who had spied on them. The first Federal Commissioner was **Joachim Gauck**, from 1990 to 2000. That is why the authority was popularly known as the **“Gauck authority”**. Gauck later became Federal President of Germany.

On **17 June 2021** the separate Stasi Records authority was dissolved. The files went to the **Federal Archives**. But they remain accessible to the people affected, researchers and the media. The archive helps people come to terms with the history of the GDR dictatorship.

gewusst: The torn-up Stasi files make up one of the biggest jigsaw puzzles in the world.
Since 1992, millions of people have applied to see Stasi records.

teile.einleitung: The Taliban are an Islamist movement in Afghanistan. They ruled from 1996 to 2001 and have been back in power since August 2021.
wichtigste: Mullah Mohammed Omar founded the Taliban in 1994.
The name means “pupils” or “students”.
Their first period of rule lasted from 1996 to 2001.
In August 2021 they took power again.
They call their state the “Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan”.
Girls may not go to school after year 6 (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: **Taliban** is the plural of **talib**, which means pupil or seeker. Many founding members came from **Koran schools** in Pakistan. **Mullah Mohammed Omar** founded the movement in 1994 in the **Kandahar** region. He hardly ever appeared in public. He died in 2013, which only became known in 2015.

From **1996 to 2001** the Taliban ruled most of Afghanistan for the first time. In 2001 they blew up the huge **Buddha statues of Bamiyan**, which were more than 1400 years old, because they reject images. After the attacks of **11 September 2001**, they were overthrown by a US-led military operation.

In **August 2021** the Taliban captured the whole country while the Western troops were withdrawing. The capital **Kabul** also fell. Kabul is in the east of the country at a height of around 1800 metres. The Taliban call their state the **“Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan”**. At its head is a religious leader.

The **Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice** checks clothing, beards and people's behaviour. Women must **cover themselves** completely in public, for example with a **burqa**. Girls may not go to school after **year 6**. The **universities** are also closed to women.

Many states and the UN criticise above all the treatment of women and girls. Most countries do not officially recognise the Taliban government. Many Afghans have fled abroad, including to Switzerland. Aid organisations are still trying to help the poor population.

gewusst: Afghanistan is the only country in the world where girls may no longer go to school after a certain age.
The Buddhas of Bamiyan were more than 1400 years old when they were blown up.

teile.einleitung: A constitution is the highest law of a state. It sets out what rights people have and where the government's power ends. Dictatorships in particular show how important it is to have a constitution that is really respected.
wichtigste: The constitution is the highest law of a state and stands above all other laws.
It sets out fundamental rights, for example freedom of expression or the right to life.
It decides how the state is organised and who has what power.
Switzerland has had a Federal Constitution since 1848; the current one has applied since 1 January 2000.
In Switzerland, every change to the constitution must be approved by the people and the cantons.
Dictators often suspend constitutions or simply ignore them.
A constitution only protects people if independent courts and free citizens defend it.

abschnitte.text: A **constitution** is something like the rules of the game for a whole country. It stands above all other laws, which is why it is also called a basic law. No ordinary law may contradict it. It sets out who governs the country, how elections work and what rights every person has.

An important part of every constitution is the **fundamental rights**. They include human dignity, freedom of expression, freedom of religion and protection from arbitrary treatment. The constitution also divides up power; this is called the **separation of powers**. Parliament, the government and the courts keep a check on each other so that nobody becomes too powerful.

Switzerland's first **Federal Constitution** came into being in 1848, when a loose confederation of states became a federal state. It was completely revised in 1874 and 1999, and the current version has applied since 1 January 2000. Every change needs a **double majority**, meaning a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons. With a popular initiative, citizens can propose a change themselves; this needs 100,000 signatures.

In a **dictatorship** there is often a constitution on paper, but it is not respected. Dictators change it so that they can stay in power longer, or suspend fundamental rights with emergency laws. This happened in Germany in 1933, when Adolf Hitler got round the Weimar Constitution with the Enabling Act. So a constitution alone is not enough: it also needs people and courts that protect it.

The **Constitution of the United States** of 1787 is one of the oldest written constitutions still in force today. In Germany the Basic Law has applied since 1949; after the experience of the Nazi period it contains especially strong fundamental rights. Great Britain, on the other hand, has no constitution in a single document. There the rules come from many laws and old traditions.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that every person has in relation to the state, such as freedom of expression.
Power in the state is shared among parliament, the government and the courts.
In Switzerland, both the people and the cantons must approve a change to the constitution.
A proposal from the people to change the constitution.

gewusst: The Swiss Federal Constitution begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”.
Because the Swiss often vote on initiatives, the constitution even contains an article about second homes.
The US Constitution has only seven articles, plus 27 amendments.

teile.einleitung: The Uyghurs are a people in north-west China. Most of them live in the Xinjiang region, where the Chinese government keeps them under heavy surveillance and has held many in camps.
wichtigste: Most Uyghurs live in Xinjiang, whose capital is Ürümqi.
They are mainly Sunni Muslims.
Uyghur is a Turkic language and is written with Arabic letters.
An estimated one million or more people have been held in camps.
China officially calls the camps vocational training centres.
Cotton from Xinjiang is criticised because of forced labour.

abschnitte.text: The **Uyghurs** live mainly in **Xinjiang** in north-west China. There they are the largest ethnic group. The capital and largest city of the region is **Ürümqi**. Xinjiang used to lie on the **Silk Road**, an old trade route between China and Europe.

Most Uyghurs are **Sunni Muslims**. **Uyghur** is a **Turkic language** and is related to Uzbek. It is written with **Arabic letters**. China severely restricts the practice of religion and the use of the language in Xinjiang.

Since 2017, according to estimates by researchers and human rights groups, **around one million or more** Uyghurs and other Muslims have been held in camps. The Chinese government officially calls them **vocational training centres**. It says that the camps serve to fight extremism. Human rights organisations speak of **re-education camps**.

In August 2022 the **UN Human Rights Office** published a report on Xinjiang. It speaks of serious human rights violations that could be **crimes against humanity**. China rejected the report. Switzerland has also expressed concern about the situation in the UN Human Rights Council.

A large part of China's **cotton** comes from Xinjiang. There are accusations that Uyghurs are forced to work there. That is why some fashion companies and countries check more carefully where their products come from. China denies the accusations of **forced labour**.

gewusst: The Uyghur language is related to Turkish, even though Turkey is thousands of kilometres away.
Xinjiang is China's largest region by area.

teile.einleitung: A state party is a party that has merged with the state and runs the state and society on its own. Other parties are banned or have to follow it.
wichtigste: A state party dominates the whole state.
Usually only its members get important posts.
The SED was formed in 1946 through the forced merger of the KPD and SPD.
The Politburo is the most important leadership body of communist parties.
The PRI governed Mexico from 1929 to 2000.
The Communist Party of China has around 100 million members (as of 2024).

abschnitte.text: In a democracy like Switzerland, many parties compete against each other, and the people decide. With a **state party** it is different. The party has **merged** closely with the state. It decides politics, the administration and often the economy too. Usually only its members get important posts.

In 1946, in the Soviet occupation zone, the **KPD** and the **SPD** were merged to form the **SED**. Many social democrats were pressured into this, which is why it is called a **forced merger**. There were other parties in the GDR, such as the GDR's CDU or the LDPD. But these **bloc parties** were not allowed to question the SED's leadership.

The most important body of a communist state party is the **Politburo**. It has only a few members but makes the most important decisions. Through the **nomenklatura**, the party decided who got leading posts in the state and the economy. In the Soviet Union, **Article 6** of the constitution guaranteed the leading role of the CPSU. Under Gorbachev this article was removed in 1990.

The **Communist Party of China** has governed the country alone since 1949. In 2024 it had around **100 million members**, making it one of the largest parties in the world. In **Mexico**, the **Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI)** provided every president from 1929 to 2000. Until 1946 it had other names. Only in 2000 did a candidate from another party win.

gewusst: The PRI dominated Mexico for more than 70 years, even though there were elections.
In the GDR, bloc parties were meant to create the appearance of variety.

teile.einleitung: The Spanish Civil War lasted from 1936 to 1939. Republicans and Nationalists fought for power, and in the end General Francisco Franco set up a dictatorship.
wichtigste: The war began in July 1936 with a military coup in Spanish Morocco.
It ended on 1 April 1939 with Franco's victory.
The Republicans defended the elected government.
Germany and Italy supported Franco.
The Soviet Union mainly helped the Republic.
Volunteers from many countries fought in the International Brigades.
Around 800 Swiss went to Spain as volunteers.

abschnitte.text: In February 1936 the **Popular Front (Frente Popular)** narrowly won the parliamentary election. This alliance included republicans, socialists and communists. The country was deeply divided politically. In July 1936 parts of the army rose up in **Spanish Morocco**. General **Francisco Franco** brought troops from there to Spain, and the coup turned into a war.

On one side were the **Republicans**, who defended the elected government. On the other side were the **Nationalists** under Franco. The Republicans defended Madrid with the cry **“No pasarán”**, which means “They shall not pass”. The politician **Dolores Ibárruri** made the cry famous.

**Hitler** sent the **Condor Legion**, and **Mussolini** several tens of thousands of soldiers. Both also tested new weapons in the process. The **Soviet Union** supplied the Republic with aircraft, tanks and advisers. France and Great Britain held back with a policy of **non-intervention**. Tens of thousands of volunteers from more than 50 countries fought for the Republic in the **International Brigades**.

Around **800 Swiss** went to Spain, most of them on the side of the Republic. Many wanted to stop fascism. Back in Switzerland, many of them were convicted of **foreign military service**, because Swiss citizens are forbidden to fight in foreign armies. Only much later were they rehabilitated by parliament.

On **1 April 1939** the war ended with Franco's victory. After that he ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975. The English writer **George Orwell** fought in a militia in Catalonia and was wounded. He wrote about it in the book **“Homage to Catalonia”**. Later he became world famous with “Animal Farm” and “Nineteen Eighty-Four”.

gewusst: The cry “No pasarán” is still used at protests in many countries today.
Many Swiss who fought in Spain were only rehabilitated by parliament in 2009.

teile.einleitung: Václav Havel was a Czech writer who opposed the communist dictatorship. For this he had to go to prison several times. After the Velvet Revolution in 1989, he became president of his country.
wichtigste: Václav Havel was born in Prague, Czechoslovakia, in 1936.
He wrote plays that the government banned.
In 1977 he co-founded the civil rights movement Charter 77.
Because of his criticism he spent almost five years in prison in total.
In November 1989 he founded the Civic Forum, and the Velvet Revolution began.
At the end of 1989 he became President of Czechoslovakia, and from 1993 to 2003 he was President of the Czech Republic.
Prague airport has borne his name since 2012.

abschnitte.text: Václav Havel was born in **Prague in 1936**. At that time his country was called **Czechoslovakia**; today it is the Czech Republic. He came from a wealthy family. After the communists took power in 1948, this was seen as a black mark. That is why the authorities refused him access to some schools.

Havel became known as a **writer**, above all for his **plays**. In them he made fun of the language and the rules of bureaucracy. After the end of the Prague Spring in 1968, his plays were banned in his own country. But they were performed abroad. Havel also wrote essays about life in a dictatorship.

In 1977 Havel and others founded **Charter 77**. This was a text in which brave people demanded that the government respect **human rights**. Those who signed it were persecuted. Havel went to **prison** several times, for almost five years in total. The communist government did not tolerate any criticism.
