In **November 1989**, a great many people took to the streets in Prague. Havel founded the **Civic Forum** to bring the protests together. The Civic Forum negotiated with the government about the change of power. After a few weeks the communist government gave up. Because the change happened almost **without violence**, it is called the **Velvet Revolution**, since velvet is a soft fabric.

At the end of **1989** Havel became **President** of Czechoslovakia. In 1993 the Czech Republic and Slovakia separated peacefully. Havel was then the first President of the Czech Republic from **1993 to 2003**. He died in 2011. Since **2012** Prague airport has been called “Letiště Václava Havla”.

gewusst: In the spring of 1989 Havel was still in prison; by the end of the same year he was president.
During the Velvet Revolution, people in the squares jingled their bunches of keys.

teile.einleitung: In a dictatorship, the government decides what is shown on television. State television always shows those in power in a good light and keeps quiet about criticism.
wichtigste: On the state television of a dictatorship, the government decides about the news.
Criticism of those in power is almost never shown.
In the GDR, the main news programme was called “Aktuelle Kamera”.
Many GDR citizens secretly watched Western television.
In North Korea, radios and televisions are fixed to state stations.
In Switzerland, radio and television are independent of the government.

abschnitte.text: In a **dictatorship**, the government controls television. It decides which news is broadcast and which is not. Criticism of those in power is not allowed. Television serves **propaganda**: it is meant to win people over to the government. Problems in the country are hushed up or blamed on others.

In the GDR, the main news programme was called **“Aktuelle Kamera”** (Current Camera). It reported things the way the state party, the **SED**, wanted. From 1960 to 1989 there was also **“Der schwarze Kanal”** (The Black Channel). The programme showed clips from Western television and ran them down. In this way viewers were meant to distrust the West.

Even so, many people in the GDR received stations from **West Germany**. To do this they turned their **aerials** towards the west. The authorities did not like this. In this way many people found out things that their own television kept quiet about. **Western television** shaped the picture that many GDR citizens had of the West.

In **North Korea**, control is especially strict. Radios and televisions are set so that people can only receive the **state stations**. In this way people only hear and see the government's messages. Receiving foreign stations is forbidden and can be severely punished.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Constitution** protects the independence of radio and television. The **Federal Council** may not decide what is shown on the news. The SRG stations are financed by licence fees, but they decide on their programmes themselves. Anyone who thinks a programme is unfair can complain to an **ombudsman office**.

gewusst: “Der schwarze Kanal” was broadcast on GDR television for almost 30 years.
Opponents mockingly called the programme “Sudel-Ede” (Smear Eddie), after the nickname of its presenter.

teile.einleitung: The Guardian Council is one of the most powerful bodies of the Islamic Republic of Iran. It checks all laws and decides who may stand in elections. This gives it great influence on the country's politics.
wichtigste: The Guardian Council has existed in Iran since the Islamic Revolution of 1979.
It has 12 members: 6 Islamic legal scholars and 6 other lawyers.
The Supreme Leader appoints the 6 clerics, and parliament elects the 6 lawyers.
Members stay in office for 6 years, and half are replaced every 3 years.
The Guardian Council checks whether laws are compatible with Islam and the constitution.
It decides who may stand in elections.
In disputes with parliament, the Expediency Council mediates.

abschnitte.text: In **1979** the Shah was overthrown in Iran. **Ayatollah Khomeini** came to power, and the **Islamic Republic** was created. Iran is regarded as a **theocracy**. The word comes from Greek and means “rule by God”. At the head of the state are clerics, above all the **Supreme Leader**. The Guardian Council is an important body under this constitution.

The Guardian Council has **12 members**. Six are **Islamic legal scholars**, whom the Supreme Leader appoints directly. The other six are **lawyers**. They are proposed by the head of the judiciary and elected by **parliament**. Members stay in office for **six years**, and half are replaced every three years.

Every law passed by the Iranian parliament must be checked by the Guardian Council. It checks whether the law is in line with the rules of **Islam** and with the **constitution**. If it is not, it sends the law back. If parliament and the Guardian Council cannot agree, the **Expediency Council** decides. This body was created in **1988**.

Anyone in Iran who wants to stand for parliament or for president must be **approved** by the Guardian Council. Very many candidates are often excluded. Critics say that voters therefore have no real choice. The government, on the other hand, stresses that the council protects the principles of the Islamic Republic. It is completely different in Switzerland: here, in principle, any person who has the right to vote may stand for election.

gewusst: The Guardian Council also oversees the election of the Assembly of Experts, which chooses the Supreme Leader.
Half of the Guardian Council is not chosen by the people but appointed directly by the Supreme Leader.

teile.einleitung: In October 1988 the people of Chile voted on whether the dictator Augusto Pinochet could continue to rule. Surprisingly, the No side won. The vote opened the way back to democracy.
wichtigste: Since the coup of 1973, General Augusto Pinochet had ruled Chile as a dictator.
In October 1988 people could vote “Sí” or “No” on eight more years of Pinochet.
No won with around 56 per cent of the vote.
The symbol of the No campaign was a colourful rainbow.
Its song was called “Chile, la alegría ya viene”, meaning “Chile, joy is coming”.
In 1989 Patricio Aylwin was elected the first freely elected president after the dictatorship.
Pinochet remained commander-in-chief of the army until 1998.

abschnitte.text: On **11 September 1973**, the military overthrew the elected president **Salvador Allende**. After that, General **Augusto Pinochet** ruled the country as a dictator. Parties were banned, and many opponents were persecuted. The **1980** constitution provided that the people would later vote on a candidate for another eight years. This vote took place in **October 1988**.

Many parties joined forces against Pinochet. Their symbol was a **rainbow**, which stood for the many different groups. The campaign relied on **cheerfulness** instead of fear. Its well-known song was called “Chile, la alegría ya viene”, meaning “Chile, joy is coming”. Both sides were allowed to show short campaign broadcasts on television every evening.

Turnout was very high. **No** received around **56 per cent**, and Yes around 44 per cent. This meant that Pinochet could not simply carry on ruling. Instead there were free elections at the end of 1989. **Patricio Aylwin** won them and took office as president in **March 1990**.

Pinochet lost the presidency but kept a lot of power. He remained commander-in-chief of the army until **1998**. After that he became a **senator for life**. In the same year he was arrested in London because a Spanish judge wanted to charge him with human rights violations. He died in 2006 without having been convicted.

In 2012 the feature film **“No”** by the Chilean director **Pablo Larraín** was released. It tells the story of an advertising man who designs the TV spots for the No campaign. The film shows how the campaign used humour and hope. It was nominated for an **Oscar** for best foreign-language film. In this way the referendum became known internationally again.

gewusst: The No side got as much television airtime as the Yes side, namely 15 minutes each per day.
It is rare for a dictator to lose power through a vote that he called himself.

teile.einleitung: Censorship means that the state controls or forbids what may appear in the media, in books or on the internet. Books, films, newspapers or websites are then banned or changed. Dictators use censorship because they do not want any criticism of their government.
wichtigste: In censorship, the state controls what may be published.
Dictators usually do not like free newspapers because they do not want criticism of the government.
In Switzerland, censorship is explicitly forbidden by the Federal Constitution.
On 10 May 1933 National Socialists in Germany burned books in public.
Today some states censor the internet and block websites.
When people stop saying anything critical out of fear, this is called self-censorship.
Age ratings for films and games are not censorship but protection of young people.

abschnitte.text: In **censorship**, an authority checks texts, pictures or films and decides whether they may appear. Unwanted passages are cut or whole works are banned. A distinction is made between **prior censorship**, in which things are checked before publication, and subsequent censorship, in which works are banned afterwards. This greatly restricts the freedom to say what you think.

Books were already being banned in the Middle Ages and the early modern period. From 1559 to 1966 the Catholic Church kept a list of forbidden books, the **Index**. On 10 May 1933 National Socialists in many German cities burned books by Jewish and critical authors. In the Soviet Union and the GDR too, only what the party allowed could be published.

Dictators want to decide what people think. That is why **independent newspapers** are closed and critical journalists are arrested. Television then mainly shows **propaganda** that praises the government. Many people stay silent out of fear, even if they disagree.

Some states today block websites, social networks or search engines. China has built a huge filtering system known as the **Great Firewall**. There, for example, many Western platforms cannot be reached. Some people get round such blocks with tools such as VPNs, which is forbidden in some countries.

Article 17 of the Federal Constitution says clearly: “Censorship is prohibited.” But **freedom of expression** has limits, for example in the case of insults, defamation or calls to hatred. During the Second World War there was also press control by the army in Switzerland. Age ratings for films and video games protect children and do not count as censorship.

begriffe.erklaerung: The state checking a work before it may be published.
When someone, out of fear, chooses not to say or write anything critical.
Deliberately influencing people through one-sided information.
The right to say and spread your own opinion freely.

gewusst: In Berlin in 1933, the writer Erich Kästner himself watched his own books being burned.
The word censorship comes from the Latin “censor”, an official in ancient Rome who, among other things, watched over public morals.
In some countries, even certain children's books or cartoon characters are banned because they are considered politically dangerous.

teile.einleitung: In an enforced disappearance, a person is secretly arrested by the state and nobody finds out where they are. Their relatives often do not know for years whether the person is still alive. Today it is regarded as a serious crime and is forbidden without exception by a UN convention.
wichtigste: In an enforced disappearance, someone is held in secret and their whereabouts are concealed.
The Night and Fog Decree of 1941 is seen as an early example.
In 2006 the UN General Assembly adopted a convention against enforced disappearance.
The convention came into force in 2010.
Systematic enforced disappearance is regarded as a crime against humanity.
A great many people disappeared during the Argentine military dictatorship.

abschnitte.text: In an **enforced disappearance**, the police, the military or other state bodies arrest a person. Afterwards they deny the arrest or conceal where the person is. Those affected have no protection from the law and the courts. Their families live in great uncertainty. This uncertainty is also meant to intimidate other people.

In **December 1941** Adolf Hitler issued the **Night and Fog Decree**. Resistance fighters from occupied territories were secretly taken to Germany. Their relatives learned nothing about their fate. The complete uncertainty was meant to deter others from resisting. The decree is regarded as an early example of state enforced disappearance.

During **Argentina's military dictatorship** from 1976 to 1983, a great many people disappeared, especially critics of the government. Many were killed, and their bodies were never meant to be found. An officer who was involved, **Adolfo Scilingo**, made the so-called **death flights** public in 1995. The mothers of the disappeared protested for years in the Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires. There were such crimes in other countries of Latin America too.

In 2013 a Syrian military photographer with the code name **“Caesar”** fled with tens of thousands of photos from the prisons of the Assad regime. The pictures prove the deaths of many people who had disappeared. The USA later named a sanctions law after him. In **China** there is a measure under which suspects can be held in a secret place for up to six months. Human rights organisations see this as a legalised form of enforced disappearance.

In **December 2006**, the UN General Assembly adopted the **International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance**. It came into force in 2010 and forbids enforced disappearance without exception. Switzerland has also joined it. Under the **Rome Statute** of the International Criminal Court, systematic enforced disappearance is regarded as a **crime against humanity**. The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva helps families to search for missing relatives.

gewusst: 30 August is the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.
The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo wore white headscarves as their symbol.

teile.einleitung: A sham election looks like a real election but is not one. People do go to the polls, but there is no real choice, no secret ballot, or the result has been decided beforehand. Dictatorships use sham elections to give themselves a democratic appearance.
wichtigste: In sham elections there is no real choice.
Results of almost 100 per cent approval are typical.
In the GDR there was only a single list.
In North Korea there is usually only one candidate per constituency.
Often there is no secret ballot.
The OSCE sends election observers to check elections.

abschnitte.text: In a **free election**, there are several parties or people to choose from. Everyone may say what they think and campaign. Voting is **secret**: nobody may see how someone votes. The counting is honest and can be checked. In Switzerland you can even cross names off lists or add them.

In a **sham election**, one or more of these things is missing. Often only government candidates can be chosen. Sometimes people are watched while they vote. The result is rigged or has already been decided. Results of **almost 100 per cent** are typical. In Iraq in 2002, Saddam Hussein even had himself confirmed with supposedly 100 per cent.

In the **GDR** there was only a **single list** of the National Front, and the distribution of seats was fixed in advance. Many people simply folded the ballot paper and dropped it into the ballot box; this was called **“Zettelfalten”** (folding the slip). Anyone who used the voting booth made themselves look suspicious. In the **local elections on 7 May 1989**, civil rights activists did their own counting and proved that the results had been rigged. This strengthened the protest against the government.

In **North Korea** there is usually only **one candidate** on the ballot paper per constituency. Anyone who wants to vote against has to cross out the name, which hardly anyone dares to do. In **Iran**, the **Guardian Council** checks all candidates and excludes many. As a result, often only people who are acceptable to the leadership can be chosen.

The **Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe**, **OSCE** for short, sends election observers to many countries. They check whether elections are free and fair and write reports about them. Its office for elections is in **Warsaw**. Switzerland is also a member of the OSCE.

gewusst: In the 1989 GDR local elections, the government officially reported almost 99 per cent approval.
In North Korea the reported turnout is usually almost 100 per cent.

teile.einleitung: The “fourth estate” is a name for the free media such as newspapers, radio, television and online news sites. Alongside parliament, the government and the courts, they keep a check on the powerful by informing people and uncovering wrongdoing. That is why they are usually suppressed in dictatorships.
wichtigste: Free media are regarded as the fourth estate, which keeps a check on power.
The three classic branches of power are parliament, the government and the courts.
Journalists inform people about politics and uncover mistakes and scandals.
The media are not a real branch of state power; they have no power to make laws or punish.
In Switzerland, media freedom is protected in the Federal Constitution.
The Watergate affair in the USA is a famous example of the power of the press.
Dictators control the media because they do not want criticism.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the term come from?
abschnitte.text: In 1748 the French thinker Montesquieu described the **separation of powers** into three parts: law-making, government and the courts. The press is often called an additional, fourth force. It has no official power, but it influences what people know and think. That is why people speak of the **fourth estate**.

abschnitte.titel: How do the media keep a check on power?
abschnitte.text: The media report on decisions of the government and parliament and explain them. They ask politicians critical questions. In **investigative journalism**, reporters often research for months to uncover hidden wrongdoing. Because the powerful know that the media are watching, they behave more carefully.

In 1972, men broke into the headquarters of the Democratic Party in the Watergate building in Washington. The reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the **Washington Post** found out that people around President Richard Nixon were behind it. Their reports led to investigations. In 1974 Nixon became the first US president to resign.

In Switzerland, Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees **media freedom**, and censorship is explicitly forbidden. As well as private newspapers, there is the SRG with radio and television in all four national languages. Switzerland regularly comes near the top of the Reporters Without Borders press freedom ranking. However, many local newspapers are struggling with less money because advertising is moving to the internet.

In **dictatorships**, critical newspapers are banned and journalists are arrested. There are problems in democracies too, for example when a few rich owners control many media outlets. On the internet, **false reports** also often spread faster than checked news. That is why it is important to check sources critically and to support serious media.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sharing state power among parliament, the government and the courts.
Thorough research to uncover hidden wrongdoing.
The right to report and publish opinions without state control.
False reports that are spread deliberately.

gewusst: The informant in the Watergate scandal was called “Deep Throat”; his identity only became known in 2005.
The term “fourth estate” for the press was already used in England in the 19th century.
In Switzerland, journalists in many cases do not have to reveal their sources; this is called protection of sources.
